title: Vintage Barker: New Writing in Old Bottles
abstract: While it is by now axiomatic to say that Howard Barker does not comfortably or conveniently fit into any generic categorisation, dramatic movement or school, the reasons behind this are rarely made explicit beyond Barker’s prescription that he would not join any club that would have him as a member. Nonetheless it is possible to locate Barker within particular dramaturgical genealogies, specifically considering his affiliation with two of Britain’s national theatre institutions prior to the inauguration of the Wrestling School: the unofficial confederacy of Leftist writers at the Royal Court in the 1970s and the RSC’s Warehouse Company in the late 70s and early 80s (the Wrestling School itself was an offshoot of what Jack Tinker described as the ‘national theatre of the fringe’, Joint Stock). Although Barker was therefore the beneficiary of producing and commissioning structures that prioritised the playwright as the originary point of creative emanation, in the mid-nineties this approach would become an end in itself, with the phenomenon of ‘New Writing’ becoming the prevalent determinant of play development processes designed to turn youth, rawness, contemporaneity and relevance into marketable entities. New Writing as a discourse is commonly credited as becoming dominant in two specific periods, with the Royal Court’s early artistic policy often perceived as marking its inception as an institutionally sanctioned practice and the mid-to-late 1990s and early 2000s distinguished by the repivoting of the British theatrical ecology upon new play development and the discovery of new, specifically young, writers. This chapter re-examines Barker’s positioning between these two periods, as a figure that is excluded from these taxonomies in critical comment, and yet still subject to the imposition of similar institutional pressures, commercial expectations and aesthetic predilections. The chapter suggests that while Barker’s theatre anticipated the replacement of the post-‘68 theatre of ideological persuasion with a theatre that appeals to corporeal sensation, offering no political frameworks as support or aspiration to its characters, the preponderance of New Writing was anchored in a type of naturalism to which Barker professed an allergic reaction as severe as his antipathy to politically progressive post-Brechtian dramaturgical models. The chapter argues that while the master-signifier ‘in-yer-face’, announced visceral spectacle and a generalised array of shock tactics as the radical gesture that defined the theatre of this period, with Sarah Kane’s work identified in some quarters as an exemplar of the Theatre of Catastrophe, the epithet often obscured the lack of dramaturgical innovation at the level of representational aesthetics cultivated by New Writing initiatives, with its vocabularies and methodologies of psychological realism, linearity of narrative, and social relevance. This chapter recognises the theoretical importance of Barker’s strident castigation of these precepts, even as they were inscribed as foundational principles in the discursive and material practices of New Writing.

title: Gods in the Bazaar: The Economies of Indian Calendar Art. By Kajri Jain. Durham, N.C.: Duke University Press, 2007. xii, 434 pp. $99.95 (cloth); $29.95 (paper).
abstract: One of the most recognizable features of the Indian bazaar is the brightly colored prints of gods and goddesses, gurus and film stars, babies and leaders that are sold in piles on the street and hung in virtually every shop. The study of these prints, the most ubiquitous form of popular art in India, has formed the center of a recent burgeoning of scholarship on visual culture in South Asia. Kajri Jain's long-anticipated monograph on Indian calendar art makes a major contribution to that literature by contextualizing her discussions of the forms taken by these popular prints within a larger analysis of the print as a commodity circulating in what she calls the “vernacular” space of the bazaar. Jain's book advances decisive positions on virtually every major debate about Indian visual culture while forging her own alternative social frame in which to view these objects.Like many other engagements with popular visual culture in India, Jain's study is motivated by her concern with the role that images have played in the development of Hindu nationalist politics since the 1980s. Jain observes that the effects of popular prints on their viewers are often misunderstood in analyses in the “forensic-juridical mode” favored by scholars and secular advocates (p. 12). Evaluations of the truth claims or representational value of these images can only understand their appeal as irrational. Jain contends that by shifting her focus to the qualities that prints take on as circulating objects—whether as commodities, gifts, icons, or fetishes—their efficacy can be better understood.Calendar art circulates in a domain that Jain describes as the “vernacular bazaar,” a space that developed in the colonial period to mediate between indigenous and colonial business sectors and was retooled in the postcolonial period to allow centralized production systems, such as the offset printing industry sited in Sivakashi, to supply diverse local demands. Throughout her study, Jain shows how the bazaar engages in a process of “vernacularizing capitalism,” a two-way movement whereby “vernacular constituencies” are incorporated into a “global” capitalism characterized by “bourgeois-modernist ideology” and capital is adapted to local circumstances in a “proliferation of multiple cultures of capitalism” (p. 37). Jain sees these two movements as alternating logics of “deterritorialization” and “reterritorialization,” whereby the forces of capital loosen, reconfigure, and then reattach the ties of social, symbolic, and political-economic formations.The trick of Jain's account is that, in a series of careful case studies ranging from the late nineteenth to the late twentieth centuries, she is able to show the effects that such moments of deterritorialization and reterritorialization have had on the form of popular prints themselves. In so doing, Jain offers original and creative responses to the most contentious subjects in studies of Indian visual culture, including the status of realism and naturalism, the historical roles played by Ravi Varma and Nathadwara painters, the role of vision (or darshan) in devotional practice, and the relationship between “sacred” and “secular” popular art images. In one of her most striking visual examples, Jain finds two distinct registers of signification in a 1932 M. V. Dhurandhar advertisement for Woodwards Gripe Water on the theme of Krishna the Butter Thief. In one register, perspectival naturalism develops a this-worldly narrative of motherhood and care, while in another, frontal address installs Krishna as an iconic presence. Instead of merely naming this as hybridity, Jain reads Dhurandhar's mediation of the distinction between mythic references and secular naturalism as a product of Woodwards' market address, which was meant to encompass both colonial elites and “domestic consumers of varying degrees of vernacularity” (pp. 122–23). Jain's engagement with the social place occupied by such images allows her to show the limits of accounts restricted to formal analysis while securing even more satisfying readings of calendar art itself.Jain's ethnographic research with calendar artists does similar work in reconsidering the crucial division between popular and high art. Jain shows calendar artists as thoughtfully engaged with issues of authorship, originality, and copying, as well as the status of realism. But the real work of these sections is to disrupt the narrative of secularization in art history, traced through the German aesthetic tradition back to Hegel, in order to reconsider the role played by a sacral aura in these mechanically reproduced objects. Jain engages with the anthropological literature on the fetish in order to develop an alternative explanation of the devotional power of calendar art images.In a much looser and more speculative set of chapters at the end of the monograph, Jain explores the relationship between calendar art images and other forms of visual culture. One striking reading links pornography, calendar art, and patriarchy, while, in a chapter on the shift to muscular images of Ram and Hanuman, Jain accounts for the unique role played by Amitabh Bachchan (and his wide and muscular chest) in 1970s India. These chapters are perhaps less closely argued than the first two-thirds of the book, but they show the remarkable range of Jain's framework in interpreting Indian public culture as a whole.Jain's book is lavishly illustrated with more than 150 color and black-and-white images, which are divided between photographs of calendars in use and reproductions of calendar art images drawn from many of the most important collections in India and abroad. The images are well selected, offering a more diverse sense of what constitutes calendar art than is often conveyed by less comprehensive studies.Jain is thoroughly engaged in the literatures of South Asian art history, history, and anthropology, and she makes sustained interventions in religious studies. Her book should command the attention of scholars in all of those disciplines and would be of use in both undergraduate and graduate classes studying modern South Asia. Like the work of Christopher Pinney, Tapati Guha-Thakurta, and others, the strength of Jain's account argues forcefully that an understanding of Indian visual culture is essential to an understanding of Indian public culture as a whole.

title: On German dramaturgy
abstract: In German, the word “dramaturgy” implies two meanings. Following the literal translation of the term from ancient Greek, it means the philosophical dimension of the “architecture of the action.” Dramaturgy is also the name of a function in the German theatre system. In the latter case it stands for the department of a theatre in which the dramaturg works as well as for the intellectual authority which “dramaturgy” has over the invention and communication of theatre. Because of that, the work of a dramaturg is equally multifaceted: s/he belongs to the management of the theatre and is the creative director and curator of new teams and projects. A dramaturg also edits the literary source material of the play and is the ﬁrst observer of a new production next to the director. As such s/he can add his or her opinions and interpretations to the artistic process during the rehearsals. The important place of dramaturgy in the German-speaking theatre originates from its historical birth during the eighteenth century. Lessing’s Hamburg Dramaturgy (Hamburgische Dramaturgie) was instrumental for the self-reﬂection of theatre producers and a guide for the audience to acquaint it with the new art of bourgeois theatre. The emerging bourgeoisie in the politically tattered country saw itself as unﬁt to overthrow the traditional political relations in an act similar to the French Revolution. The unique path that Germany took was often described as an escape into the arts. The art of Romanticism and the German city theatre (Stadttheater) are the two most distinctive examples of this sublimation. During the nineteenth century every city tried to build a theatre in its centre as a sign of its self-conﬁdent citizens. The performances there were of varying quality and covered every genre: opera, operetta, ballet, play, musical comedy, melodrama, etc. The thriving market for plays oﬀered a range of diﬀerent texts, so the repertoire of the city theatre could satisfy the lust for entertainment and the wish for representation even-handedly. The birth of city theatre lies in the idealism of Lessing’s Dramaturgy, which was carried on by the dramaturgies of the theatre. People worked on and are still working on the idea of theatre as a political art of self-reﬂection. This idealism combines the philosophical and institutional dimensions of dramaturgy. At the beginning of this development stands the dramaturgy of the bourgeois tragedy (Bürgerliches Trauerspiel), which sought for a diﬀerent and new relation between the audience and the theatre, other than that of the folk theatre and the French tragedy, which provided either amusement or lofty elevation. A new dramaturgy of the action as much as a new dramaturgy of the performance was needed. The new characters had to show their inner lives, which led to a new dramaturgy of the psychological action. The characters knew about, and fought against, the constraints that social conventions imposed on them. The phantasm of the natural form was in the centre of this representation. Likewise, a new kind of acting had to be invented. To demonstrate the new situation believably, the actors had to learn to play in a new way. They had to be able to show the external constraints and the internal struggles at the same time, and they had to learn to play on two diﬀerent levels at once. The characters of psychological theatre feel and reﬂect their emotions; they are looking for something and are insecure whether this desire is right. They have to conceal something and nevertheless want to be acknowledged as individuals. The identiﬁcatory potential of the new theatre consists in the fact that the audience possesses the same technique of self-expression in their everyday lives. In civic society trust arises not through conventions of role-playing and the coding of the costume as it did at court, but by showing one’s inner, true, and therefore invisible personality. But how will someone be able to show these hidden qualities if their authenticity lies in the fact that they cannot be deliberately shown? Self-expression just has to happen, has to appear unintentionally and against the will of the subject. The border of desire and suﬀering, of feeling and thinking becomes the main diﬀerence in this bourgeois dramaturgy. This is why there is so much crying and sighing in the bourgeois tragedy. These borders of the sayable give an insight into the “true” self. In this way, the aspiring bourgeois class, which wanted to experience itself as true in its own feelings, found the adequate art for its self-discovery and self-aﬃrmation in the theatre. The subject of modern history is characterized by this self-reﬂection, which became the theme and the means of the presentation in the new dramaturgy of realism. During the nineteenth century, realism and naturalism brought this new method to perfection, which in turn had an impact on the art of acting. Until the reinvention of theatre as a bourgeois art, new inventions came from theatre authors and actors and originated from ritual and traditional sources. Now a new actor enters the stage. The new style of play desired by psychological realism necessitates rehearsals during which the new eﬀects of playing behind the “fourth wall” can be reviewed. The direct contact between actor and spectator is broken; the act of representation has to be invisible. Through this new kind of play, the audience disappears for the actor as much as for the spectator him or herself. S/he is not part of the audience anymore but the only one feeling in the dark stalls. The development of this new impression requires a surrogate for this lone spectator: the director enters the theatre. The director sits in the auditorium as a representative of every future member of the audience, and next to him or her sits the dramaturg as the ﬁrst critic of the event. From here, the handling of concentration, attention, and sympathy is organized. The dramaturgy of the action is staged with the dramaturgy of a performance. The theatre text does not become theatre within a convention or a tradition of a play, but every performance becomes an original production which bestows upon the text its own form of presentation. The goal of realistic theatre was the representation of bourgeois contradictions which originated in the necessary ambiguous communication between the market and alienated labour. Because capitalism turns everything into a commodity that receives its price on the market, life gets shaped by a double alienation of work on the one hand and the negotiation of prices on the other. As the new bourgeois class experiences itself as the winner of this alienation, the art of realism loses its critical potential and becomes a form of entertainment. The once dialectical representation of the world becomes “commercial realism,” which adopts the strong eﬀect of identiﬁcatory moments without the desire of showing the contradictions behind it. The enlightening power of realistic theatre loses itself in the lulling stream of feelings which eventually ends in the cinema. In the twentieth century, epic theatre turns against this tendency by taking the self- reference of the modern subject seriously. It re-establishes the contradiction as the foundation of a dialectical theatre. According to Brecht, the simplest deﬁnition of the epic manner of acting is the actor showing one thing while at the same time showing him or herself. By doing so, s/he establishes a relationship between showing and what is shown as well as between the one showing and the spectator. By this, the dispositive of the fourth wall gets abolished, the once direct contact, which characterized folk theatre, is established again and is expanded by the dimension of a reﬂecting actor. For dramaturgy, the epic theatre has far-ranging consequences. The architecture of the epic scene is diﬀerent from the dramatic situation insofar as it is no longer written to create suspense or a sense of identiﬁcation but for the act of showing. Likewise, the dramaturgy of a performance is no longer built towards a closed story arc (geschlossener Wirkungsbogen) but for the demonstration of certain aspects of the contradiction. The contradiction of the drama, which started the need for the characters to act, becomes the contradiction in society which the exemplary presentation shall make understandable by the exemplary presentation of speciﬁc facts. Therefore, the dramaturg’s collaboration during the rehearsals is no longer limited to aesthetic questions but broadens into the horizon of the social relevance of the theatrical event: how are the social contradictions reﬂected in human souls and bodies? The consequences of the political demand placed on theatre are hardly to be overemphasized for the German-speaking theatre system. They are connected to the enlightened idea of theatre as the art of an emancipated middle class as much as to the ideological feuds of the twentieth century. As a result of this, the dramaturg moves again to the center of the intermediation between theatre and reality. The rehearsals become enriched by his or her research, which subsequently becomes available for the audience in the form of the theatre program. The dramaturg’s vision, which is marked by the attitude of “include me out,” becomes the touchstone of social relevance. The art of epic theatre thereby frees itself from the desperate attempt of late bourgeois art to be meaningful because of the artist’s uniqueness, while rediscovering collective work as the natural state of theatre. The ramiﬁcations of psychological and epic theatre are similar for German theatre, but since the 1980s they have become increasingly overlaid by postmodern theory. This development operates under the name of the “postdramatic” but assembles numerous and sometimes contradictory characteristics of a postmodern theatre. Two manifestations of postdramatic theatre can be roughly distinguished. On the one hand, it stands in the tradition of visual arts, especially that of the early-twentieth-century avant-garde. This can be seen in the use of collages, which cause sensory and semantic eﬀects from the clash of unexpected materials. In this way, the dramaturgy of the performance no longer is structured by the dramatic action but by energetic, rhythmic, and other aesthetic phenomena. In this case, the dramaturg is not so much a mediator between the ﬁctional world of the drama, the reality of the performances, and the social presence as the co-author of a fable of the production that needs reinvention. Through the abandonment of the dramatic structure, the collective presence, as evoked by theatre, changes. One can say that dramatic theatre produces a community of feeling and identifying spectators whose presence is sentimental because it is directed backwards. On the other hand, epic theatre in contrast produces a community of astonished spectators, who come to know the familiar as strange in order to experience the changeability of the world as possible. Their present is coined by a faith in the future. The postdramatic theatre produces pictorial puzzles in which the audience can no longer decide whether what they are seeing is a sensual irritation or a semantic eﬀect, whether it is play or reality, whether it is meant or it really happens. This oscillation in perception generates a special form of presence. The self-reference of the modern subject, which is always experienced as a relation between at least two conﬂicting levels, becomes an aesthetical paradox of a selfreferent perception. Thus, the presence of perception becomes aware of itself and expands into a broader presence. One perceives and realizes one’s own perception at the same time. In this way, the broad presence lays itself over the past and the possible future. The oscillations of postdramatic theatre become a feast of self-referentiality in which the contradictions are no longer psychologically or socially justiﬁed but rather become aesthetic games. The other tendency of postdramatic theatre derives not so much from visual arts but from Brecht, to the extent that it could also be called post-epic theatre. Here, the play on two diﬀerent levels, as Brecht asked for, gets adopted, but without having recourse to the social position of the actor. It is no longer the political individual that tries to become aware of his or her class and, emancipated, stands in front of the audience, now the performer makes his or her own presence become the foundation of the stage presence. As a result, the techniques of realistic acting become mostly expendable because of the mimetic ability of creating a diﬀerent situation on stage so that the actual theatre situation is no longer necessary. The actor becomes a performer, which means that s/he enters the stage not as an acting subject but as one who is experiencing the world and reality. The performer is the always responsive employee that emotional capitalism demands. The dramaturgy of such a post-epic performance evolves from the scenic material which emerges during the rehearsals. There is no dramatic template from which the eﬀect and structure of the dramatic arc could be developed, but the scenic inventions must be composed by their diﬀerent dimensions. The dramaturgic assistance here becomes the central authority of artistic invention, requiring not only the techniques of drama but also the eﬀects of mash-ups, music, and dance, to arrange the speciﬁc material into something more than a scenic essay about a certain topic. The speciﬁc character of scenic inventions and the deliberate approach to them are part of postepic theatre. Because of this, the self-referentiality of the scene becomes central again, which previously – in its performative form – had its roots in performance art and in poststructuralism. During the performance, the scenic reality acquired an intrinsic value, because of self-referential plays and their continuity. Through this, the material emerges from behind the semiotic dimension. In poststructuralism, the sign becomes analyzed in view of its intrinsic value. Its power to signify something covers that which is hereby signiﬁed. Through the practice of such a deconstruction, all certainties crumble into discursive games. In a postmodern theatre that is critical towards representation, both techniques are often practiced. The categories of drama, mimesis, and catharsis as a banishment of spectators, who unite to form an audience in order to experience theatre as a collective, become replaced by the postmodern categories of self-reference, performance, and paradox. The diversity of the diﬀerent dramaturgic techniques is striking. In German theatre, all four traditions (dramatic, epic, postdramatic and post-epic) exist simultaneously, and the lines between oﬃcial city theatres and independent theatres become increasingly blurred. As a result, not only actors have to expand their skills. Above all, dramaturgy always has to invent and comprehend new architectures of actions and eﬀects. This variety of theatrical expressions has wide-ranging consequences for the education of young dramaturgs. There are two diﬀerent training routes in the German-speaking theatre. One runs through art colleges where dramaturgy is taught alongside acting, scenery, costume design, and directing. The other route is through theatre studies, which has diverse oﬀers in applied theatre studies. In this case, what is taught is not a speciﬁc skill but a theoretical understanding of theatre and theatrical events. As the foundation of applied theatre studies fell into the high phase of postmodern cultural theories, their aesthetic paradigms have been highly marked by them. The openness of the scientiﬁc education still dissociates itself from the classical, technical art forms of theatre and its mimetic claim. Applied theatre studies fosters a remarkable alliance of virtuosic perception, discursive processing, and production of new forms of theatre. The accusation that theatre is produced purely for theatre studies is certainly true for some of these self-referential formats. The production of more and more essay collections, which elevate a just-seen performance to the level of indispensable knowledge of the ﬁeld, surely fuels this cycle further. It cannot be overlooked that the innovative energy of the technical theatre education is in danger of weakening and that the forms inspired by these discourses frequently appear more modern and animated. Since public attention to theatre is rather diminishing, we have to ask whether this animosity is really useful, especially since this strong diﬀerentiation only furthers the exhaustion of mimetic energy and the encapsulation of postmodern aesthetics towards a complacent game. The prime task of the dramaturgs and dramaturgies is to build a connection between the dramatic art and the more discursive theatre. What is needed for this purpose is an intense engagement with the technical-mimetic side of theatre as much as with the discursive procedure. Such an engagement, however, has to break through the dividing barriers instead of getting entangled in more ﬁghts for distinction. And whose job would be more appropriate for this than that of the mediator, the dramaturg?

title: Five Directors: Auteurism from Assayas to Ozon Five Directors: Auteurism from Assayas to Ozon. Edited by K. I nce . Manchester, Manchester University Press, 2008. x + 158 pp. Hb £45.00.
abstract: Despite the deliberate vagueness of its main title, this volume offers a powerful reassessment of the auteur tradition in contemporary Francophone cinema, specifically the work of Olivier Assayas, Jacques Audiard, the Dardenne brothers, Michael Haneke and François Ozon. The obvious charge that this is an all-male line-up—all the more odd if one considers that some of the most powerful cinema in French is currently being produced by female directors like Claire Denis and Catherine Breillat—is pre-empted by the editor's statement that another book on women directors was in preparation with Manchester University Press at the same time. In a succinct and efficient introduction, the editor argues for a more nuanced and capacious conception of engaged auteurism that puts into question the earlier male heroics of the Nouvelle Vague and moves firmly beyond normative heterosexual conceptions of the family. The five essays included all extend these key points in different ways. Martin O'Shaughnessy provides an incisive study of the changing nature of political commitment in the post-industrial project of the Dardenne brothers, from the early documentaries to the later fictions that produce a shift from the ethico-political to the purely ethical. Paul Sutton explores the ‘catastrophic mode’ and contradictory presentation of reality in Assayas's films, although the argument is perhaps too much determined by the views of another critic. Ince's own contribution traces Ozon's treatment of the couple and shows how the notion of ‘home’ is reinvented as ‘a place open to a radical transformation of patriarchy, a queer and unpredictable space that invites new and unspecified social formations’ (p. 126). This is a sensitive account, yet the assertion that Ozon is ‘France's first mainstream queer auteur’ (p. 113), as if Cocteau had never existed, remains problematic. The most far-reaching and illuminating chapters are those by Julia Dobson and Libby Saxton on Audiard and Haneke respectively. Dobson analyses the auteurist trope of filiation and the contestatory approach to realism in Audiard's work, arguing very persuasively that it goes beyond standard notions of both filial relations and the hierarchical assumptions of auteurism in favour of change and reinvention. Saxton's complex, multi-layered and beautifully written chapter on Haneke gets to the core of his provocative work, namely the manipulation of the viewer. Through impressive close readings of films like Caché, Saxton offers a bold interpretation of a director who deconstructs the illusions of mediated suffering encouraged by the media in an attempt to give back to violence what it truly is (i.e. pain to another). Haneke is revealed to be attuned to the ‘fragile, transitory, liquid ethical bonds which survive in a diegetic reality where intersubjective relations are increasingly mediated by technology’ (p. 86). A photograph of Haneke on set provides the cover image, but otherwise this volume is sadly devoid of illustrations. Rounded off by a brief conclusion, more a coda, the collection as a whole will be of greatest interest to students, although researchers already familiar with the directors featured will also find much to engage with and admire.

title: Social Class and Television Drama in Contemporary Britain
abstract: Class has always been at the heart of the television crime drama. Whether it is the post-war paternalism of Dixon of Dock Green (1955 – 1976), the harsh social realism of The Sweeney (1975-1978), or the almost mythical evocations of Britain in Heartbeat (1992 – 2010) and Midsomer Murders (1997- present), class and crime have always been seen as being inextricably linked. Since the 1990s, the British crime drama has been influenced by successive waves of cultural imports from, firstly, the US and then from Scandinavia. There is now a recognisable ‘genre’ for what we might think of as British TV Noir. Beginning with shows such as Cracker (1993 – 2006), Prime Suspect (1991 – 2006) and Messiah (2001) and continuing with dramas like Red Riding (2008), Southcliffe (2013) and Hinterland (2013 – present), the British TV Noir employs narratives and stylistic tropes that might usually be associated with the cinema of the 1940s. Although drawing influence from high profile shows such as Twin Peaks (1990 – 1991), Millennium (1996) and (latterly) The Wire (2002 – 2008), CSI (2000 – present) and The Killing (2007) these British Noir shows also articulate the nation’s shifting class system. As Susan Sydney-Smith has ably demonstrated, the crime drama is “historically contingent” (Sydney-Smith, 2002, p. 5) and shaped by the surrounding socio-political, as well aesthetic, context. To this end, this chapter traces the depiction of class in three key crime series – Prime Suspect, Red Riding and Southcliffe - and explores how social class, and more importantly, its changing face provides a constant background to the narratives and characterisations. These three texts were each produced at pivotal moments in Britain’s relationship to class – Prime Suspect was shown 6 months after Margaret Thatcher vacated office; Red Riding was produced in the midst of the global recession in 2008 and Southcliffe was made in the shadows of stringing welfare and immigration reforms. These texts span three successive political administrations and over two decades of social and political change. Understanding the relationship between criminal activity and class in these dramas however is far more complicated than simply reading the historical context through the text. Commensurate with its cinematic incarnation, TV Noir is both reflective and productive, employing visual and narrative tropes to manipulate, as well reflect, its audience’s moral and social positioning. The picture that emerges from an examination of class and the British TV Noir is one of suspicion and discontent. As Andrew Spicer suggests (with reference to British cinema) the Noir sensibility both depicts and critiques a society that it sees as being “class-ridden, racist and misogynist” (Spicer, 2002, p.202). This is certainly the case with the texts that are being examined here, as social positions and taxonomies are constantly being redefined and renegotiated.

title: Lumiere's Arrival of the Train: Cinema's Founding Myth
abstract: [End Page 89] Today, we cannot comprehend the terror that gripped the 1895 audience facing the Lumière brothers' arriving train—this first film with which they gave birth to documentary film.1 Louis Lumière's film Arrival of the Train shows, in only fifty seconds, an everyday occurrence, a familiar experience for spectators: a train pulls into a station, the passengers go back and forth on the platform. Despite its brevity and the banality of its subject matter, this film has attained fame, entering film history as an icon of the medium's origins. Just how important the film had become in constructing the founding myth of cinema's birth became clear during the centenary of cinema, which provided ample opportunity to recall the film. In Germany, as well as in other countries, numerous television and press reports attested to cinema's undiminished vitality, using this film as evidence: already pronounced dead several times, cinema was said to be capable of resisting even new electronic media by asserting its peculiar power to fascinate the senses and to appeal to audiences. In this context, Lumière's cinematographic locomotive and its startling effect is mentioned repeatedly as an illuminating example from the first days of cinema. Thus, Hellmuth Karasek writes in Der Spiegel: One short film had a particularly lasting impact; yes, it caused fear, terror, even panic....It was the film L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de la Ciotat (Arrival of the Train at La Ciotat Station)....Although the cinematographic train was dashing toward the crowded audience in flickering black and white (not in natural colors and natural dimensions), and although the only sound accompanying it was the monotonous clatter of the projector's sprockets engaging into the film's perforation, the spectators felt physically threatened and panicked.2 Even the German Railway's customer magazine picks up the gag, visually embellishing the supposedly panicky reaction: "The spectators ran out of the hall in terror because the locomotive headed right for them. They feared that it could plunge off the screen and onto them."3 The Munich Abendzeitung purportedly knew that "at the time, people, appalled by Arrival of the Train, were said to have leaped from their chairs."4 These journalistic claims are of course backed up by the standard works of film history. In Gregor and Patalas we can read that "according to handed-down knowledge, the locomotive terrified the audience."5 In connection with the menacing effect of Nosferatu, Lotte Eisner recalls that "the spectators in the Grand Café involuntarily threw [End Page 90] themselves back in their seats in fright, because Lumière's giant locomotive pulling into the station seemingly ran toward them."6 Georges Sadoul, in his French classic of film history, writes: "In L'Arrivée d'un train, the locomotive, coming from the background of the screen, rushed toward the spectators, who jumped up in shock, as they feared getting run over."7 It is beside the point that these standard works were written thirty to forty years ago. The audience's terror in view of the arriving train is still passed on as a proven fact by film historians today. Bernard Chardère laconically notes, "The locomotive frightened the spectators."8 In the German edition of Emmanuelle Toulet's Birth of the Motion Picture, one can read under the heading "Beginning with Terror": "The amazement at seeing windswept trees and stormy seas is followed by naked horror when the train approaching the station of La Ciotat appears to move toward them."9 Noël Burch also asserts that in 1896 the spectators "jumped up from their chairs in shock."10 Finally, Jean-Jacques Meusy simply assumes that these audience reactions are known and presents Arrival of the Train as the spectacular beginning of the medium's affective power: "The overwhelming realism of this film is proof of the complete identification of...

title: Committed Cinema: The Films of Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne. Essays and Interviews Committed Cinema: The Films of Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne. Essays and Interviews. Edited by B ert C ardullo . Newcastle upon Tyne: Cambridge Scholars Publishing, 2009. xvi + 218 pp., pl., ill. Hb £39.99.
abstract: The Dardenne brothers are amongst the most important contemporary European filmmakers. The little known early part of their filmmaking career was devoted to documenting collective leftist resistances in their native Belgium, but they are now known worldwide for the succession of intense, compelling fictions which began with La Promesse (1996) and which explore the violence of the current socio-economic order with relentless intensity but without ever giving in to despair. This volume is the first book-length study in English to deal with their works. Pulling together previously published material from British and American sources, it combines a series of longer essays and shorter reviews by notable critics such as Jonathan Rosenbaum, Robin Wood, and Gerald Peary with a generous number of interviews with the brothers themselves. The latter form the most consistently impressive part of the book, for the brothers are always insightful and incisive as they discuss their influences, their working practices, and their own understanding of their films. The essays and reviews are less strong in their impact, not because they are weak individually — many are very perceptive — but because they often tend to cover similar ground, as when, for example, they repeatedly summarize the brothers' early career. Due to their greater length, the essays take analyses further and are generally more satisfying than the reviews. Doug Cummings's piece, ‘The Brothers Dardenne: Responding to the Face of the Other’, gives a particularly insightful account of the brothers' Levinas-influenced, face-to-face aesthetic and its capacity to combine obsessive proximity to the characters with a respect for their alterity. David Walsh's essay is less persuasive, but nonetheless poses the essential question of the political value of the brothers' films. Given the book's title, this is a question that hangs over the work as a whole, one that the brothers themselves tend to dismiss or answer obliquely. Walsh is very critical but not always fair: he seems to want the films to develop the kind of explicit critique of the contemporary order that would strip them of much of their claustrophobic intensity. He also reads them in terms of psychological and narrative realism, failing to see that, rather than having conventional plots, they dramatize ethical dilemmas as they play out across characters who cannot therefore be understood in psychological terms. Yet his key criticism, that the films propose ethico-moral responses to socio-economic problems, is surely worth exploration. In the most recent review, Jim Wolfreys comments: ‘Few directors are capable today of depicting the human cost of capitalism's brutality with the simple force and eloquence of the Dardenne brothers’ (p. 122). His comments balance Walsh's critique without entirely invalidating it. Overall, the book is a very useful source. Clearly not a substitute for the fully developed analysis that a book-length study would allow, it is full of insights and usefully documents critical responses to the brothers' works, especially in the United States, where their films are seen to provide welcome relief from standard Hollywood fare.

title: SEDIVY, SONIA. Beauty and the End of Art: Wittgenstein, Plurality and Perception. London: Bloomsbury Academic, 2016, x + 258 pp., 8 b&w illus., £85.00 cloth.
abstract: This book is impressive for its command of the material, its scope, and its vision. What looks at first to be a rehash of the “end of art” debate, along with comments about a rising interest in the concept of beauty, ends up being a wide‐ranging reappropriation of Wittgenstein via McDowell, Kant, and Dewey to construct an understanding of art in terms of practices, perceptual engagement, and plurality. Along the way, Sedivy has some interesting things to say about such well‐known figures as Danto, Belting, Gadamer, Scarry, Nehamas, Hickey, Walton, and Gerhard Richter, a detail of one of whose paintings graces the cover of the book. In the first chapter, Sedivy questions Danto's “end of art” thesis along with the essentialism upon which it is based, although she agrees with Danto about the historical nature of art and that we have entered into a new era of pluralism. The second chapter turns to “beauty,” with a focus on Gadamer's concepts of play, symbol, and festival. She concludes that one cannot understand art's nature without taking into account beautiful art and that beautiful art needs a theory of perception that explains rule‐governed and culturally determined experience (p. 57). The third chapter continues on the theme of beauty and individuality, focusing on Scarry, Nehamas, and Hickey. Scarry suggests that beauty, exemplified by Matisse's Nice paintings, gives us what she calls “capacious consciousness,” and that appreciation of perceptible structure in beautiful objects can “call” us to promote “the good.” Whereas Scarry stresses perception, Nehamas emphasizes interpretation by way of his paradigm of Manet's Olympia. Sedivy, however, is more impressed by Hickey's approach to beauty, particularly his focus on oil glazing in the Renaissance and the resulting layers of luminosity which become, he believes, a metaphor for grace. She sees this as fleshing out Danto's definition of art as embodiment of meaning, noting that Danto himself refers to great paintings as having a mystery of light and a curious grace (p. 81). This may sound religious, but Sedivy agrees with her authors that there is no transcendental backing for such experience. We reach the tentative conclusion that beauty might be a value we should reaffirm for art (p. 90). Part II, which starts with a chapter on art from a Wittgensteinian perspective, focuses on norms in context. Sedivy's interpretation of Wittgenstein is based on McDowell's realism. Art is a set of norm‐governed practices, and the force of these norms is specific to such practices, hence requiring historical knowledge to understand them. This is presented as an alternative to the essentialism of Danto and Levinson. Although an anti‐essentialist, Sedivy rejects Weitz's neo‐Wittgensteinian family resemblance position in favor of Wittgenstein's metaphor of a thread, the strength of which consists of the overlapping of many fibers (p. 118). In line with this, she argues for a “Wittgensteinian realist” orientation to art with an emphasis on “forms of life” and with special regard to how these are constituted by contingent historical facts of the sort historians like Linda Nochlin have explored. It is the norms of art that give identity to the works and activities of art, and art properties are bound to historical contingencies related to the norms of local art practices (p. 126). Chapter 5 turns to the relation between art practices and perceptual engagement. It also begins to develop Sedivy's central notion of “conceptual realism.” She starts off by quoting Dewey on the wonder experienced when the live creature encounters perceptual qualities while participating in the ongoings of the surrounding world (p. 149). She then synthesizes the Wittgensteinian notion of “forms of life” with Dewey's idea of perceptual engagement. She agrees with Dewey that art practices elaborate and diversify the life activity of perception. She also finds accord between her approach and Walton's idea that some aesthetic properties depend on historical categories of art. Aware that conceptual art might pose a problem for her perceptualism, she concedes that constitutive norms of art need not be aesthetic. Chapter 6 turns to beauty as the value of perceptible presence. She does this by way of a sympathetic discussion of Kant. Sedivy argues, perhaps as a departure from Kant, that beauty is a value that admits plurality. The chapter continues with an argument against aesthetic supervenience as a solution to the problem of objective evaluation. (Her conceptual realism is supposed to do that job.) It ends with rejection of the view that the beauty of art is just a consolation best avoided in times of social injustice. After discussing Scruton and Danto on this topic, Sedivy finds resolution again in Hickey's idea of grace as visible. In her concluding chapter she defines beauty as “the value of the world's perceptible presence” (p. 239) and asserts that we need to consider “the distinctive nature of perceptual engagement if we are to understand beauty and art” (p. 240). This book should be read by everyone specializing in philosophy of art or aesthetics. Sedivy's position is complex and subtle, and, although I will be raising some criticisms, my overall impression is highly positive. Few books in recent years have made me think so much. I agree with many of her views, for example, with rejecting definitions of art in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions, with denying the relevance of supervenience theory to aesthetics, and with opposing the end‐of‐art thesis (while still recognizing that we need to deal with a feeling of ending). I also agree with the importance she places on the concept of beauty. I am more skeptical of her “conceptual realism,” mainly because I think this position prompts her to shortchange the role that metaphorical thinking plays both in art and in philosophy. The problem I have with her position can be summed up by the following contrast. Sedivy holds that “because perception engages us with the determinate characteristics of particular individuals [etc.] perceptual experience is itself of value and perceptual presence has value” (p. 170). I would rather say that because “perception,” which I take to include imaginative perception and “seeing as” and not just sense access to objective external properties (Dewey's “experience” works better in this regard), engages us with the indeterminate characteristics of particular individuals as covered by what Kant called “aesthetic ideas” (as well as determinate characteristics), perceptual experience is of value. Although Sedivy does pay considerable attention to Kant on “aesthetic ideas” she seems unaware that, for Kant, the fine artist is no conformist to conventional rules or even to “the world” but creates his or her own world out of materials taken from nature (#49 Critique of Judgment). I have a similar problem with Sedivy on Wittgenstein. Although her interpretation of his material on language games and family resemblance is fine, she neglects the other idea much mentioned in the literature of aesthetics, that of “seeing as” discussed in Part II of Philosophical Investigations. In this, she leaves out an essential aspect of aesthetic seeing, which involves not so much seeing under a concept (McDowell) or category (Walton) as seeing contrary to a concept or category: that is, metaphorical seeing. And because of this, she over‐emphasizes rule following (seeming to favor the first part of Philosophical Investigations over the second). Interestingly, Danto himself picked up on the importance of “seeing as” when he argued that the “is” of artistic identification, exemplified by the boy who sees a stick as a horse, is a necessary condition for art, a point which she also misses (1964. “The Artworld,” The Journal of Philosophy 61: 571–584). In short, rule breaking is as important in art as rule following. I have a related problem with Sedivy's version of historicism. Hers is a standard form entirely oriented toward the existence of past context, which itself is treated as though it, and its categories, were fixed. A fuller form of historicism recognizes that historical categories themselves are subject to competing interpretations, even to change. This form is opposed to only focusing on the past and looks at how the past is taken up into the present. Gadamer, whom Sedivy follows in other respects, favors this sort of historicism when he talks of “fusion of horizons.” Dewey's historicism is even richer since it takes into account how past and present are reshaped in accord with an envisioned future. Further, since Sedivy rejects meta‐narratives, she has no account of how competing practices can, together, induce change. The idea of dialectic (as in Hegel, Marx, Dewey, Danto, and, most importantly here, Weitz) is needed here. Although Sedivy sometimes talks about the evolution of art she, unlike Weitz, does not provide any account of the engine of that evolution. For Weitz, evolution of art theory (and perhaps also of art) is based on competing honorific definitions of art. He implicitly suggests we look at the history of art and of culture in terms of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis, in which competing definitions, and the paradigms that give them content, are determinative. We should only resist meta‐narratives for art if these are taken as absolute. Artists and philosophers still need to tell stories about the history of art, and these stories will still tend to have a dialectical structure. Similarly, we still need theory, even if the theories are disguised honorific definitions, each one offered in response to previous ones. This leads to my main criticism of Sedivy's handling of Weitz. Basically, she does not take into account his main point. For Weitz, even though “art” is a concept that cannot be defined in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions, theory still has a role in aesthetics. On his view, previous theories of art were not actually definitions of art in terms of necessary and sufficient conditions but honorific definitions, or redefinitions of art in terms of preferred properties. These are disguised recommendations for what we should attend to in art. When Bell says that “art is significant form” he is best interpreted as saying that artists and art critics should attend to relations between lines and colors that give us the experience of what he calls aesthetic “rapture.” Paradigms play an important role in theory change, although Weitz does not fully articulate this. Paradigms were important for most of the classical definitions of art (which, again, Weitz sees as disguised honorific definitions). For example, Bell took Cézanne as his paradigm, and Danto took Warhol's Brillo Boxes as his. Sedivy rejects the importance of paradigms because they do not play a central role in Wittgenstein and because she thinks references to paradigms may be eliminated (p. 144). But Sedivy may not be as far from Weitz as she thinks, for it is arguable that she herself is offering, although unaware of it, an honorific definition of art with its own paradigm. Her project could be divided into two parts. The first depends on Wittgenstein's thread analogy. Rather than defining art, this approach tells us that art is an interconnected set of practices. But, as Sedivy is aware, this does not distinguish art from other interconnected sets of practices, for example from sports. This leads to the second part of her approach. Here she offers what seems to be an honorific definition of art. To elaborate, sometimes (for instance in textbooks) honorific definitions appear in shorthand using the term “as.” For example, Bell's definition may be represented as “art as significant form,” Plato's as “art as imitation,” Dickie's as “art as institutional” and Dewey's as “art as experience.” These can all be seen as metaphorical definitions, that is, not literal definitions of “real” essences, but capturing, in different ways and at different times, the evolving nature of art. Sedivy's honorific definition might be described as “art as engaged perception” or perhaps, more simply, “art as beautiful.” Since such shorthand definitions are metaphorical it does not matter in this case that not all art is perceptual or beautiful. Only through such a definition (granted, she would not call it such) can she deal with what she calls the “horizon of the present” (p. 1). That is, an honorific definition has the advantage of being able to deal cogently with the current cultural situation. And, as Weitz argued, paradigms play an important role here. Just as Bell made his theory more concrete with frequent mentions of the post‐Impressionists, similarly, for Sedivy, Gerhard Richter is paradigmatic. His work exemplifies a level of perceptual richness and complexity that brings forth the importance of beauty that she wishes to highlight in her (implicit) honorific definition of art (p. 197). Reading what she has to say about Richter is a large part of what makes this book exciting. Hers is a good honorific definition with a good paradigm. Sedivy's implicit honorific definition can be seen as in the tradition of Dewey. Like Arnold Berleant before her (1993. Art And Engagement. Temple University Press), Sedivy stresses art as perceptual engagement. As mentioned above, she features a quote from Dewey about sensation as participation in the wonder and splendor of the world (p. 149). Also, like Dewey, she stresses the relationship between art and everyday life. This is exemplified by her discussion of the way one perceives the colors of leaves and items in store windows on an imagined walk (p. 151). A Deweyan pragmatist would say, “so far, so good!” However, her description of this walk seems idiosyncratic. And this leads to a further problem. As Sedivy puts it, she always sees “an individual belonging to a kind or an instance of a property that I see” (p. 151) and, in seeing leaves, “I see a range of highly similar shades of green repeat hundredfold” (p. 151). She insists that “one's experience always individuates what one sees in terms of some higher‐order kind or other” (p. 151), which is what she means by “seeing determinately.” That is, she believes that in seeing leaves we always see their determinate shades and hues. Yet in my experience walking in the woods, in a mall, or in an art gallery, kinds do not play an important role. I do not say to myself “this is a red rose” and so forth. And, as an amateur plein air watercolorist, I just do not experience all of this classification and determinacy when looking at the leaves I paint. At least for me, language (as in classification according to kind) plays a minimal role in the aesthetic experiences of a silent walk. This is not to say that kinds and concepts do not play an important role unconsciously. But I am not convinced that classification plays as strong a role as Sedivy thinks it does, even on the unconscious level. Sure, to perceive an individual is to grasp what makes it what it is, but, contra Sedivy, this must go beyond merely classifying it (162). Of course as soon as I think about speaking or writing, then kinds, and the words that describe them, become important. But a lot of experience is beneath that level (cf. Richard Shusterman. 1990. “Beneath Interpretation.” The Monist 73: 181–204). Moreover, Sedivy's description of a walk in the woods fails to capture either the historical or the imaginative dimensions of such experience. Indeed, she seems a kind of formalist with respect to natural and everyday aesthetic experience, focusing only on surface perceptual properties, unlike her approach to art, which at least incorporates historical context. Finally, a problem comes up with Sedivy's concept of “second nature,” and this has to do with theory of creativity. She introduces this concept in the context of rule following and training (p. 106), but later takes it to refer to our freedom to choose (p. 210). The early passages seem, on first reading, inconsistent with the later. For example, in the early part, Wittgenstein is approvingly quoted as saying “When I obey a rule, I do not choose. I obey the rule blindly” (p. 106), which directly contradicts the idea of choice. Further, Sedivy agrees with Meredith Williams that a child is “calibrated … to the world through training into activities and judgments integral to the activities” (p. 106). The child is seen as like a standard of measurement that is “engraved and scored” (p. 106). Although this may be true at the level of first learning how to make judgments like “this is red,” it would not seem helpful for understanding the creative process or art appreciation. Similarly, this kind of talk might work for academic art but probably not for creative art. One wonders how the child can ever break away from this conformist world posited by Wittgensteinian “realists” and create anything new. Sedivy also claims that such “training does not involve alternative interpretations” (p. 108) and that allowing for alternative interpretations comes with a “world picture that is ‘disastrous’ for realism” (p. 108). One is tempted to reply, so much the worse for this sort of realism. By the end of the book it becomes clear that such training provides a basis for freedom, freedom based on choice. And, as Sedivy puts it, “free choice requires a background of largely correct judgement” (p. 211). But what kinds of judgment are these, and what kind of choice is allowed? Is the claim, that Chartres's stained‐glass windows are marvelous, to be lined up in the “largely correct” pile? Is this really the role that such judgments play in the language game of evaluation? Granted, it is an objective fact that medieval European people valued stained glass, and art historians can tell us a lot about this. But this is not enough to ground normative objectivity. It does not tell us that this stained glass window is a masterpiece or what it means to say so in a particular context. The freedom Sedivy posits is freedom to choose only from a vast sea of preexistent values and judgments, “a banquet of choices” (p. 211) that becomes available. This is what she means by pluralism. It is not the freedom of the Kantian artist who creates indeterminate concepts and makes worlds. It allows no real creativity since the field of values from which one can choose is preexistent.

title: Weaving Democracy
abstract: The lost thread of Jacques Rancière's title is an overdetermined signifier, itself an interwoven history. Most obviously, it refers to the loss of the authority of plot as derived from Aristotelian aesthetics. Aristotle redeemed literature from Plato's accusation of delusive falsehood by asserting that the artist's delineation of the rational chain of cause and effect was a superior form of truth to the historian's mere succession of facts. Subsequently, this order of rationality conferred the authority of its form of truth on philosophical and scientific discourse and on the social and political sciences. In the field of literature, rational verisimilitude produced a totalizing aesthetic in which only some people were designated capable of meaningful speech and action, dignified feelings, and motivation toward a noble goal. All those not privileged with the status of rationality were relegated to the order of noise rather than speech and their lives ruled by repetition as opposed to the heroic capacity for willed action.Much of Rancière's critical writing has delineated the destruction of this classical order of verisimilitude. The political, social, and aesthetic energies that constituted a turmoil of forces at the end of the eighteenth century overwhelmed the rational order of causal plot and its demarcation of who may and may not speak and act meaningfully. A new democratic aesthetic regime broke free in which anyone can say anything at all and in which any aspect of the world whatsoever became worthy of writing. Rancière claims that in place of the causal thread of plot as imposition of singular meaning and truth, a redistribution of sensible reality imposed itself. Instead of an idealist rational hierarchy, material existence comes to be understood as multiple, nonhierarchal, interwoven, and infinite. The rational thread of absolute truth is replaced by a plurality of verbal texture.Yet in many ways, Rancière's greater concern is with another loss. He argues that the aesthetic democratic revolution within literature has been misinterpreted by literary critics almost since its inception. Contemporary readers of early nineteenth-century realists criticized the mass of detail that flooded their texts as detrimental to aesthetic decorum. Subsequent critics, from Walter Benjamin to Roland Barthes, interpreted the new textual multiplicity of writing as a symptom of materialist excess, an obsessive compulsion to affirm the solidity of the bourgeois world as the only possible reality. The pursuit of art for art's sake was a means by which artists broke free from the claims of an overburdening materialism. Structuralist and poststructuralist writers likewise severed textuality from the sensible world. What gets completely lost in this long critical tradition of disdain for descriptive detail is recognition of the revolutionary potential of the aesthetic embrace of materiality. Rancière challenges this consensual judgment against physical matter. It is the excess of the sensible, he argues, that overthrows the old representational plot of action that had sustained classical verisimilitude. In its place an egalitarian inclusiveness and sensory inexhaustibility became, from the late eighteenth century, the defining quality of a new aesthetic regime.Undoubtedly, this is a revisionary account offering quite new ways of approaching realism and modernism, without a sense of binary opposition and without rejection of materialism. For Rancière, both realism and modernism need to be understood as participating in a democratic aesthetic that redistributes the perceptible world, ceaselessly expanding the horizons of the sensible. The structuring perception of the new aesthetic, replacing the linear drive of causality and action, is what Rancière terms the “lived fabric of a world,” an inclusive, interactive web of material reality (15). In The Lost Thread, he discusses the work of Flaubert, Conrad, and Woolf, whose narrative dynamics variously express a struggle for dominance between plot as imposition of hierarchical rationality, on one hand, and the unbounded textuality of a sensory realm on the other. In the second part of the book, Rancière analyzes the poetry of Keats and Baudelaire in terms of a republican aspiration of human creativity. A final essay on theater returns to the tension between political aspirations born of the revolutionary era and forms of artistic production. How is the new aesthetic dissensus to be expressed as understanding that can inform political thought and action without reinscribing it as a form of knowledge and thereby reinvesting in the tyranny of plot?Dissensus has been a central term in accounts of Rancière's writing, designating his focus upon points of fracture within political and aesthetic consensus. In particular, he argues that an egalitarian surge of sensory existence into the novel form around the end of the eighteenth century has its counterpart in the refusal of ordinary working people to stay within the scope of life and ambitions previously allotted them. The old consensuses of artistic decorum and social relations were both swept aside. In The Lost Thread, however, Rancière is somewhat less focused upon moments of dissensus than upon processes of transformational encounters between residual and revolutionary aesthetics. In his multifaceted analysis of texts, he seeks to uncover the political work of a new radical sensibility inherent in the form itself, regardless of content. While Emma Bovary's romantic dreams can be aligned with the aspirations of workers for emancipation from drudgery, the plot of Emma's story enacts no heroic enlargement. In general, while the new aesthetic regime is empowered by the sweep of multiple sensory reality into the textual life of art, Rancière argues, realist plots seal off democratic victories from their characters. Flaubert splits Emma into two aesthetic parts. One form of her imagined being enacts a condensation of the impersonal, teeming sensory fabric of life, the endless atoms of experience her body encounters. This is the verbal triumph of the new radical aesthetic; but the character knows her life only in terms of the old representative order, even while no longer retaining the freedom of heroic action. The nineteenth-century realists appropriated the egalitarian power of dissensus but sacrificed their characters to the plot, Rancière claims.Conrad shares the late nineteenth-century philosophical skepticism as to universal truths. Thus for him, the authority of plot is weakened. Conrad's stories, Rancière argues, arise from a mistaken assumption, illusion, or belief. The skepticism is textual in scope; the mass of verbal detail destroys the possibility of any final singular meaning. The texts of novels like Lord Jim enact a narrative decomposition into fragmented microscopic events. No finite resolution can limit the unending flow of a sensible world. But the novel as genre demands plot. In Lord Jim, an entirely arbitrary conclusion is simply imposed. In Heart of Darkness, Marlow's lie radically betrays Conrad's new egalitarian aesthetics of infinite textuality. The sheer magnitude of sensible existence that Conrad infuses into his stories and their distance from routine life preclude any ending commensurate with that vastness.Perhaps, Rancière suggests, the lesson is to shift the immensities of sky and space to the domestic sphere. Which is what Virginia Woolf does, he claims. All of Woolf's novels, he argues, articulate a tension between plot and a new aesthetic of nonexclusive multiplicity. The evocation of the radical otherness of sensible processes in the middle section of To the Lighthouse is curtailed by enclosure within the female plot of the first section and the father's plot in the final section. In Mrs. Dalloway, the dialectic between singularity and multiplicity is more integrated by means of anonymous subjectivities spread across city space. The narrative, likewise, disperses plot across multiple trajectories.Nevertheless, one might argue that Woolf's practice is more radical than Rancière recognizes. While Emma Bovary as character is split from consciousness of her being as sensory existence, Woolf's female characters inhabit that split as consciousness. They live simultaneously within the great democracy of the sensible world and within the consensual plots of power and subordination. As such they constitute a continuous force of dissensus throughout the text. Furthermore, far from domesticating the immensity of the sensible fabric of life, Woolf's verbal heterogeneity reconfigures consensual values of scale; material reality is a continuum encompassing atoms and stars, nerve fibers and tidal movement, discarded boots, traditional nursery rhymes, and the splatter of mud.Keats's engagement with the contentious politics of his time has long divided critical opinion: are his sympathies with radical causes or with the pursuit of an ideal of timeless beauty? Rancière's reading, focusing largely upon Ode to Autumn, argues that Keats's politics are inherent in his aesthetic practice. Rancière foregrounds the activity of art as weaving in opposition to the singularity of plot. Few poets, he claims, felt as powerfully as Keats that poetry is an interweaving of contraries: the material and the immaterial, passivity and activity. For Keats, the interwoven fabric that constitutes a poem brings into being a multiple community of existing poems, fragments of sound like birdsong, remembered images and words, and poems only entertained in reveries. This perception of the whole sensible fabric of existence underlying poetic sensibility projects a possible new human relationship of shared creativity. It is the form of egalitarian politics constituting Keats's verse. Keats's affirmation of negative capability refutes the traditional hierarchy in which only some are born to noble action and words and the many to mere existence. By refusing poetic individualism and annulling the difference between activity and reverie, Keats's poetic radicalism affirms a communal creativity unendingly interweaving all aspects of life. Keats thus participates in the great democratic upheavals, recognizing the capacity of the many to engage in the “diligent indolence” of art that will establish a community of equals (75).Baudelaire's radicalism, like that of Keats, inheres within his aesthetic practice, Rancière claims. Such a view directly challenges Benjamin's influential reading of Baudelaire. For such critics, Baudelaire gives powerful expression to the dehumanizing, sordid emptiness experienced by the fleeting crowds on city streets. His poetry voices alienation, not community. But Baudelaire's response is more complex, Rancière suggests, and derives from a Balzacian sense of human life so vast and varied that any Aristotelian rational causation founders. It is not so much that the modern world has become too prosaic as that it has become too immense to sustain plot. Baudelaire's poems enact encounters between subjects who are networks of sensation within a sensible world that has no limit.The poetic apprehension of this multiplicity requires a form of “reverie,” not as inwardness but as an erasure of any boundary between inside and outside. The poem is necessarily a fragment of this unstable, floating existence, a “patch of sky seen through the basement window” (105). As such, Baudelaire's verse sustains neither individualized Aristotelian subjectivity nor yet the singularity of pantheistic universal life. It is the multiplicity of sensible existence inhering in each glimpsed sight, each feeling, each momentary sensation of Baudelaire's poetic practice that offers itself, Rancière says, to “the aesthetic Republic's work of infinitization” (113). Baudelaire's complex response to the city recognizes its rapaciousness, its sordid appetites, but equally and positively grasps its poetic participation in a new democratic redistribution that erases the identifying boundaries of beauty, ugliness, sin, and grace. It is in the mutations, divisions, and contradictions of multiple life and multiple lives that “the idea of poetry and the Republic combined to draw a certain visage of community” (113).Rancière's account of the aesthetic transformations stemming from the revolutionary era brings a welcome challenge to the political skepticism that has dominated literary studies, especially in regard to realism. In that sense, his work is itself a project of dissensus, a redistribution of the perceptible of a new aesthetic regime. It is a regime that radically reconfigures the sensible world as an egalitarian, horizontal continuity beyond any possibility of completion. Neither is dissensus ever a completed project. The politics of aesthetics is not the acquiring of knowledge. It is a transformational redistributive practice. Thus Woolf shatters the consensual scale inscribing degrees of importance and relevance. Poets project a republican vision of creative community, sustained by a new sensibility of the infinite fabric of life. Within the current political world, across almost all consensual regimes, the plots of truth have hardened into hostile dogmas. One must hope that a sense of the multiply interwoven experiences, microevents, and epoch changes that constitute the material fabric of life will empower an aesthetic dissensus—not an Aristotelian realism but a recognition of the radical, egalitarian implications of inhabiting a shared sensory world, “the great democracy of sensible coexistences” (13).

title: Hollywood film, 1963-1976: years of revolution and reaction
