title: Hegel, moderniste? Remarks on Robert Pippin's After the Beautiful
abstract: Robert Pippin's After the Beautiful presents a case for the continuing relevance of Hegel's aesthetic theory and of more broadly Hegelian approaches to the philosophy of art.1 As is characteristic of Pippin's work, the book is both illuminating and a rich source for further reflection. Pippin's case relies on restricting certain of Hegel's philosophical views, and the restrictions in question are not trivial. In particular, Hegel's claim that art no longer can have a leading or even significant role in increased human self‐understanding and in the realization of freedom must be set aside (pp. 35–39). Such negative pronouncements on the part of Hegel concerning art's continued viability for modern European self‐understanding simply have not stood the test of time. So, Pippin holds that, going forward, the Hegelian should treat such attitudes on the part of Hegel as extrusions of an overly strict, teleological conception of dialectic. One must liberate Hegelianism, that is, from the letter of Hegel's dialectic and so from his statements that art has ended—first, with respect to its role as a leading vehicle of human self‐knowledge in classical Greece and, second, in terms of its very ability to convey further self‐knowledge with romanticism. Divorcing dialectic from overarching teleology is in effect the only Hegelian thing to do if Hegel's dialectical conception of self‐determination (Selbstbestimmung) is to gain purchase in the discussion of modern art. More specifically Pippin is concerned to understand in Hegelian terms modern European painting roughly from the realism of Courbet and Manet to post‐impressionism. Pippin refers to this as a period of “pictorial modernism.” I take it that this phrase is to be understood as an abbreviated genitive that one should read both “subjectively” and “objectively.” That is, pictorial modernism is both the modernism of pictorial art (genitivus obiectivus = how modernism is expressed via the pictorial arts) and a specific kind of modernism (genitivus subiectivus = how modernism more generally is pictorial). Although Pippin does not quite come out and say it, After the Beautiful forwards a competitor to the mainstream way of charting the development of modern pictorial art (and other modern art as well) in terms of its increasing musicality. This conception of the development of art in the period under consideration, which one finds in different forms in Schelling, Schopenhauer, Wagner, Nietzsche, and Adorno, is a species of the Renaissance practice of paragone, taking the move from figural art to abstraction to be more indicative of what counts as “modern.” But it is not exactly silent on Pippin's favorite examples of French realism. It is important to note that the musicality hypothesis is compatible with certain aspects of Hegel's aesthetic progressivism, for instance, with the idea that one mode of art goads inferior modes into replicating imperfectly the advanced effects and structures of the superior mode. So, I am not sure Pippin wants to reject the musicality thesis outright and replace it with his concentration on pictorial modernism as a leading edge or whether he holds that they can complement one another. Prima facie the contrast between the two ways of thinking about modern art promises to be stark. For the musicality theorist the central concern is releasing subjectivity from the normative confines of the social and natural world through procedures of figural abstraction and summoning forth the Dionysian unconscious. The subjectivity primarily at issue here is not one pre‐adapted to sociality but rather one that increases its depth by radically restructuring reality in its own terms. This project has its clear antecedents in romanticism, as many scholars have recognized. In contrast, Pippin's Hegel will valorize realism—a position the historical Hegel would certainly have appreciated—and the idea of mutual recognition, not a breaking of the social vessels, is central. So, while Pippin is careful to restrict his specific case for the continuing relevance of Hegel's philosophy of art to the time period extending from what many art historians take to be the emergence of modern painting in Manet in the 1860s to the stirrings of figural abstraction in Cézanne's Bathers from the first decade of the twentieth century, there is even more at stake. Hegel of course did not live to see modern Europe. If one were to take as authoritative Hegel's statements at the conclusion of his lectures on aesthetics, one would not have much to go on in developing an account of modernism. One would be left with an extension of Dutch portraiture or with what Hegel calls in his treatment of poetry “true” or “objective” humor.2 It is my sense that Pippin takes his cue very much from the former. The latter is not a very exciting category by modernist lights.3 How one moves on from Hegel in a yet recognizably Hegelian vein raises questions both of (A) whether one can isolate sufficiently the results of the dialectic from the teleological dialectical apparatus and (B) if one can do so, which elements of dialectic one would feature going forward. I agree with Pippin that Hegel's own view generally is that Geist is in a position to certify to itself that it has achieved in principle full reconciliation with aspects of the world, it, and the relation of world to it, that were otherwise alienating. Hegel makes this claim for theoretical closure at a level of philosophical analysis that he considers much more advanced than the consideration of art—that is, at the level of the final and culminating form of what he calls “Absolute Spirit,” that is, “Philosophy.” “Art” is also a form of Absolute Spirit, one that is subordinate to Philosophy, and the impact of full reconciliation and theoretical closure on it follows from the subordination. Art's “end” for Hegel is, in that sense, a technical result internal to Hegel's theory of Absolute Spirit. Pippin does not argue for (A) above but finds himself in a long line of neo‐Hegelians in holding that releasing the teleological constraints of Hegel's own conception of dialectic as they operate at the overarching architectonic level does not present any special problem with preserving a recognizably Hegelian conception of dialectical rationality. He is also in neo‐Hegelian company in answering (B), in finding the conception of recognition to be a key to advancing “what lives,” as Croce put it, of Hegel.4 What is required to advance Hegel's views into modernity is a sense of recognition with ample room for alienation, that is, what one might call a Hegelian sense of failed recognition. And that is precisely what Pippin provides. Before one gets to the topic of recognition, two preliminary matters of reconstruction seem crucial for Pippin. The first is to preserve Hegel's historicism, especially as it intersects with another element of his thought: his rejection of a strict concept/percept division. Hegel treats the concept/percept binary contextually. The binary is theoretically permissible and even necessary and progressive given certain background assumptions. But if one were to ask whether ultimately there is a divide in theory or experience between categorial thought and cognitive receptivity, the answer for Hegel clearly would be that there is no such division. Second, Hegel analyzes action as a full‐fledged and, in many ways, basic form of thought. In particular, bodily action of forming objects is thinking, as is the bodily action of forming things whose main point is that they be seen as expressing the action constitutive of their making—for instance, art. It is worthwhile at this point to step back from Hegel's own doctrines in order to motivate via a more neutral medium how they might be extended in the artistic cases Pippin discusses. Hegel views art as inherently dealing in sensuously embedded concepts. That art is conceptual means that it is a form of Geist’s self‐expression and self‐knowledge; that it is sensuous is what makes it the form of Absolute Spirit that it is over and against other such forms. What is at issue here is visual art and sight; more specifically, what is at stake is how sight might be a form of conceptual life. Now, there is an approach to perception when it comes to considering sense modalities and their relation to more articulating modes of cognition that holds that sense modalities an sich and at their basic level are impervious to conceptual articulation. Sensuous perception on this account is passive in its receptivity, and whatever role it has in conceptually articulated experience is given to it “down the line” by higher order, conceptual modes of experience: one can and does (quite a lot of the time) see without thinking. But this is not the only approach to perception. One might instead argue that seeing is dependent on looking. To say that seeing is dependent on looking is to say that to see X one needs to orient one's sight with regard to X—that is, that seeing X requires an intentional action of bringing sight to X. Given this, one might informally summarize an argument for the ascription of recognition at a pre‐predicative or pre‐reflective level of visual experience as follows: Looking is an intentional activity, that is, one which operates even at the point of its minimal specification in terms of something like “choice.” Intentional activities, even at minimal levels of their specifications, are already cognitively structured and, so, are pre‐adapted to further structuring by intentional content of a more developed sort (for instance, beliefs). Seeing requires looking. Seeing is always intentional. Seeing, because intentional itself, is pre‐adapted to structuring in terms of more developed intentional content. I believe Hegel would accept something like this account of vision and its relation to looking and its inherent conceptual articulation, and I take it that Pippin would agree (pp. 41–42, 49–50). The conclusion of the argument is compatible with treating perception as embodied; Merleau‐Ponty is a kind of Hegelian in this sense. It is also compatible with treating the conceptual articulation of perceptual states as a matter of the concepts that are available for such structuring at different points in history. That said, it is easy to see that, while the argument establishes a potential basis for grafting the structure of Hegelian recognition to pre‐reflective visual states that form the basis for an aesthetic, sensuous dimension, by itself it is insufficient to do so. It is simply not specific enough. For one thing, from the fact that seeing involves looking and from the fact that looking involves at least some minimal sense of regard for the thing looked at, one cannot draw any immediate conclusion concerning whether such regard will be positive, negative, or in between. Even assuming that what is looked at is another looker, that does not without more entail that the regard is a kind of recognition, which in the Hegelian vein is certainly not neutral and in most cases operates according to at least a tacit ideal of positive mutual regard. (Of course, in some of the most famous of his cases, Hegel attempts to show that mutual antagonistic regard is the product of at least the stirrings of, say, respect.) Nor does the conclusion of the argument entail that the regard, be it positive or negative, would provide an impetus to sustained interaction between one who is looking, on the one hand, and what or whom is being looked at, on the other. That the thing looked at is itself a looker also does not guarantee this result without more said about the relation of looking, the nature of lookers, or both. But here again it seems that ordinary experience can help the Hegelian out a bit, for looking and being looked at do seem to be basically experientially and conceptually interrelated. Soon after a child can look she is aware that she can be looked at, and this awareness infiltrates and forms her looking in terms of her being looked at. This is a signal structure for the Hegelian, as Pippin emphasizes, for the reciprocity of seeing qua looking now can be further specified in terms of recognition and its application to at least visual art that makes the combination of looking and being looked at thematic, and some modernist visual art clearly has that brief. For, once one allows that seeing has intentional structure ab initio, it is open to one to argue that this intentional base can be modeled in various sorts of personal, social, and historical ways by interpenetrating conceptual resources. That is, the idea of intention here plays a structural role within an account of perception that facilitates what one might call the reciprocal ‘travel’ of cognitive resources from the more generically articulated to the less and from the less to the more. As Pippin writes in the introductory sections of the book, this picture is implied but not very well worked out by Kant (pp. 9–15); Hegel's epistemology makes it central by emphasizing the importance of the historical constitution of such resources.5 Of course, none of this structure uniquely supports the progressive historical story Hegelians often tell about such resources or the idea that reconciliation is always a tacit ideal of recognition. Hegelians will have to argue for the merits of those ideas independently. This is the point at which recognition can reenter the story. Ordinarily recognition is an explicit and fully conceptual action; one would not ordinarily say that seeing without more involves the sort of regard that typifies Hegelian recognition. “Recognition” is a social–moral category for him that, if it has work to do at the perceptual/sensuous level, will involve various relatively conceptually inarticulate ways of looking and being looked at. Take Manet's Olympia. The painting is both a mediation and provocation concerning canons of looking at nudes. The titular figure looks at one looking at her as a nude; her look says, depending on one's interpretation, “what are you looking at?” “what are you looking at?” or “why are looking at all?”6 Her look defies that of the onlooker, thereby placing in question the art‐historical project of making objects that solicit the kinds of looking that female nudes typically do. T. J. Clark's treatment of the Olympia and of other of Manet's works strikes me as especially convincing.7 As Clark sees things, the painting is in dialogue with both the historical practice of painting nudes (compare Manet's reference to Titian's Venus of Urbino) as well as with the “low” material culture of its day. Michael Fried has argued that one such source is the contemporary practice of photographing prostitutes for pornographic purposes.8 Alexander Nehamas extends the point in holding that the painting is of such a photographic session.9 Nehamas's more explicit reference to photography overreaches; it is more plausible and powerful to view Manet's painting as painting not of a photographic session but under the aesthetic style of such photography, as Fried suggests. Nevertheless, concentration on photography as a normative presence in the work is brilliant in unmasking the particular kind of pretention that Olympia's look foregrounds. Its focus on the encroachment of exchange relations (prostitutes, pornographic postcards) into easel painting is of a piece with Clark's insistence that, if one looks hard enough at scenes of middle‐ and lower middle‐class leisure painted in impressionism, one sees factories and other modes of advancing industrialization. For Clark, the appeal to “flatness” that features, say, in Greenberg's account of abstract expressionism and Fry's of post‐impressionism gains in social weight in Manet's case; the flatness of the canvas is a very specific sort—the flatness of such photographs. One tries to look at Olympia under the duplicitous guise of the nude—as if looking at her were anything but buying her for erotic use. Her look at that looking—the way being looked at is directed back at the audience—disabuses one of the fiction. She does not merely look at or past one; rather she looks through one. title: GAL, MICHALLE. Aestheticism: Deep Formalism and the Emergence of Modernist Aesthetics. Bern, Switzerland: Peter Lang AG International Academic Publishers, 2015, 166 pp., 6 color illus., $60.95 paper.
abstract: Has the development of analytic aesthetics in the twentieth century led us astray? Michalle Gal suggests it has in her new book Aestheticism. Gal's thesis and theory are simultaneously radical and familiar. She seeks to reconstruct and reassert a modernist aesthetic theory (which includes a theory of the essence of art) from the late nineteenth century and early twentieth century with some alterations and amendments. In doing so, she rehearses the history of two related moments in art, art theorizing, and criticism: aestheticism and formalism. She demonstrates that these two theories are fecund for the construction of a new theory. Gal judiciously uses quotations from primary sources (Whistler, Pater, Wilde, Fry, Bell), and very helpful color plates (six) of paintings by Whistler, Albert Moore, Henry Landseer, and Jasper Johns. Gal attempts to rescue aestheticism and early formalism from the typical criticism that these theories are too extreme (or superficial) with respect to their concentration on formal and surface qualities. From the beginning of the book, Gal sets up a foil to her new theory: what she calls “linguistic aesthetics or symbolic aesthetics.” By this she means the influence of the philosophy of language (inter alia) on twentieth century, analytic (or Anglo‐American) aesthetics. Gal begins by discussing the famous Whistler versus Ruskin trial of 1878. She finds the issues broached in this trial instructive. Ruskin represents the pre‐modernist, mimetic view of art, while Whistler is coming to terms with what will eventually develop into aestheticism and early formalism. Chapter 1 broaches the merger of content and form and the practical anti‐realism of aestheticism‐formalism. Practical anti‐realism involves the recognition of art as a “detached and autonomous ontological sphere” (p. 18), and thereby liberation from the mimetic, realist representation of nature and the world. Aestheticists prescribe that artists must develop “cultivated blindness”: non‐naturalism as artificiality, i.e., they must create an autonomous, internal order in art, not an imitation of natural order. In addition, Gal discusses “untranslatability” of external meanings or ideas from one medium to another, which implies the uniqueness of each artistic medium, and thereby the dichotomy of form and content dissolves. Chapter 2 begins with an interesting discussion of the distinction between visual and conceptual mimesis. Visual mimesis is the pre‐modern, traditional definition of mimesis. Conceptual mimesis, which is a product of linguistic aesthetics, is committed to the idea that form and content are separable. The artwork becomes (centrally) an intellectual object, not a sensual one. The artwork becomes complete when interpreted by the viewer or critic. In addition, this conceptual mimesis permits the inversion of what aestheticism considers internal and external properties of an artwork. According to Gal, linguistic aesthetic theory claims that an artwork is a “symbol whose core essence lies in its content” (p. 13). She claims that once one determines content as the essence, this leads to “translation” problems. Contents may be expressed in different media—e.g., sound (music), text (literature), color and shape (painting)—or from one artwork to another. For example, if a poem can be paraphrased (“translated”), what is paraphrased or summarized is its content. Aestheticist‐formalists disagree that this can be achieved; it requires a misunderstanding of the nature of an artwork. Putting aside other issues in aesthetic epistemology and testimony, one might as well read the CliffsNotes. Also in Chapter 2, Gal introduces two important concepts for her aestheticism‐formalism: “introversiveness” and “un‐recruitability.” (Some of the terminology Gal uses and coins is cumbersome.) Introversive art absorbs external properties or referents into the form. “Cultural charge” is already “materially dwelling in the form” (p. 64). I take “cultural charge” to be an amalgam of symbolic meanings, codes, thematic meanings, and associations that people discern or infer from certain formal properties and materials. Introversion is also important in establishing artistic freedom, which is derived (perhaps paradoxically) from the artist's self‐restraint in adhering to the limits and requirements of the medium being used. This is in juxtaposition to the notion of artistic freedom in linguistic aesthetic theory, which locates freedom in expansionism—stretching the limits of the various media (e.g., theatrical works without narrative, music without sound). It may be similar to claiming that excessive freedom is no freedom at all; freedom must exist within a framework of constraints. “Un‐recruitability” refers to art being “structurally immune to external conquest” (p. 100). For example, artificial beauty is not supposed to remind the spectator of natural beauty. Content is fused to form, and they cannot be separated. These concepts, along with untranslatability, sound like a strong form of medium‐specificity. Mysteriously, the now common term “medium‐specificity” is not used. Introversiveness and un‐recruitability account for the autonomy of art. Furthermore, prescriptively, an artist has obligations to the requirements and limitations of the medium in which she works, but she has no external obligations (this is part of the meaning of the dictum “art for art's sake” associated with aestheticism). Chapter 3 addresses the concept of syntacticity and musicality. Syntacticity is the internal arrangement of material within an artwork. Here, there is disagreement among the aestheticians themselves. Wilde argues that the literary arts are the highest among art forms; Pater argues that music is the highest; and Whistler argues that painting is the highest. Probably this debate is pointless, but the point of attempting such hierarchies here is worthwhile. Because of the aestheticist‐formalist goal to privilege the internal order and arrangement of materials in art, music becomes the best example of how this can be achieved. Music then functions as an analogy to how the other art forms can achieve a kind of “musicality.” Chapter 4 discusses the way in which aestheticism‐formalism divorces art from life—it seeks a detachment of one from the other that helps to emphasize artificiality in art. In one important section, Gal attempts to explicate her concept of “deep form”—a central concept in the book. Pinning it down is difficult. From what I can gather, deep form consists in the artwork's formal properties imbued with some combination of aesthetic and artistic properties. In the last chapter, Gal says: “Accordingly, deep form is such that it absorbs material and non‐material elements as content, meaning, idea, and thought. The form renders non‐material elements unextractable from it and subordinated to its internal arrangement. Thus they, in turn, render the form deep” (p. 152). In chapter 5, Gal explains the concept of the “completeness” of the artwork in aestheticism. Completeness of an artwork consists in internal order, ontological independence, and a particular conception of beauty. Chapter 6 addresses the nature and role of criticism. Gal claims that criticism plays two roles in aestheticism. First, criticism enforces the limits of media. Second, criticism gives rise to new artworks. On this view, criticism does not interpret artworks, but encourages new ones. The reception of art consists in absorption and a focus on experience, not the extraction of cognitive value. Art is primarily spirit edification. Gal's combination of altered elements from aestheticism and early formalism is called deep formalism, which is intended to be a complete theory of art. This includes a definition of the artwork as deep form. Thus, the essential features of an artwork are opacity, un‐recruitability, introversiveness, non‐reflective yet productive symbolism, freedom, and completeness. Other terms may serve Gal's theoretical goals more effectively and would reduce the inelegance of some of these neologisms. Currently, there are terms that could have been employed with suitable modifications (e.g., medium‐specificity, autonomism). Often it is difficult to determine the boundaries of these concepts, if there are boundaries. If there are no strict differences in meaning, then the surfeit of concepts is puzzling. At the end of chapter 3, Gal offers an interpretation of Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest. The play is meant to serve as an exemplar for the aestheticist‐formalist artwork par excellence and to demonstrate the workings of the theory. To claim that the play is about Victorian manners and mores (“referential manifesto against the hypocrisy of Victorian social conduct” [p. 84]) already misunderstands the artwork. The problem inheres in the idea that “the play is about …” What follows “about” is some meaning (or referring to) that is external to the “world” of the play itself. According to Gal and her aestheticist‐formalist allies, interpreting artworks in this way has a cost: the ignoring or devaluing of the formal features of the artwork, its artificiality, and perhaps, most importantly, such a reading causes misunderstanding of the artwork's essential features. One wonders precisely why the two critical practices are opposed, or why one denigrates the other. Focusing on both the formal properties of the play and its thematic meaning are useful in interpreting the play; both methods can produce true statements about the play, and, for the most part, one can be put forward without negating the other. But is it plausible to believe that Wilde intended the play to be about language only? Gal argues that Wilde did, and cites some of Wilde's own criticism that substantiates this claim. Some critics might reply that the critique of language is (or is analogous to) the critique of codes. In other words, the play addresses both language and Victorian social conduct. One might even be tempted to say that the one serves the other. But therein lies the rub. When there is such a division in possible interpretations, there is an inclination to say that the aestheticist‐formalist one serves the thematic one (external content). Once again, form is subordinated to content. Thus, Gal supports the idea that the play meets all of the aestheticist‐formalist criteria and therefore has no separable content. If the last line of the play (“I've now realized for the first time in my life the vital Importance of Being Earnest”) is referring to the word “earnest” (both as an adjective and twice as a proper noun [title of the play, name], which is achieved through homonymic ambiguity by its being uttered in performance), then one cannot claim without contradiction that “Earnest” refers to the rigid designator of the name “Earnest.” Gal makes the case that even the characters of Gwendolyn and Cecily possess anti‐realist theories of language. They want to marry men named “Earnest.” They care about the name only. When one posits that one artistic goal serves another, namely, that form serves content, then one is privileging the one function of art that also makes art's existence problematic. This is exactly the situation that aestheticism‐formalism criticizes and rejects. Gal begins the last chapter with a question: “Why did modernism in aesthetics collapse?” (p. 145). Did it collapse, or did it transform or evolve? Furthermore, there is a difference between modernist art evolving, or at least giving rise to, new kinds of art, new genres, etc., and modernist aesthetic theory being discredited, refuted, or at least developed into a presumably more cogent aesthetic theory. Since the first‐order art changed, the theory had to change with it. Besides, this diagnosis seems to suppose that there is a unified, consensus theory of art in the rarefied world of aesthetics. Obviously, that is not the case. Another potential shortcoming is that Gal relies exclusively on two philosophers for her exposition of linguistic aesthetics or symbolic aesthetics: Nelson Goodman and Arthur Danto. Obviously and justifiably, Goodman and Danto are pillars of contemporary aesthetics. Nonetheless, I think most aestheticians would find using Goodman's and Danto's work as emblematic of analytic aesthetics as too narrow and certainly insufficient for making generalizations about analytic aesthetics and/or this historical period of aesthetics. To be fair, analytic aesthetics is not necessarily equivalent to what Gal calls linguistic aesthetics—linguistic aesthetics may be one sub‐part or version of analytic aesthetics. Certainly analytic aesthetics developed from the significant foundations Goodman and Danto provided, but there are many other sources—and many significantly different from Goodman and Danto (one thinks of Wollheim). While there is no doubt that the philosophy of language has influenced every branch of philosophy in the twentieth century, this influence, especially in aesthetics, has not resulted in a universal or unified treatment or application of the linguistic concepts and tools. For example, Gal objects to the notion of symbol in linguistic aesthetics, external/internal distinction, and reliance upon an artwork's relationship to external referents, concerns, and values. Gal is suggesting that the tenets of aestheticism and early formalism better reflect what artists do or should do (more on that in a moment). In linguistic aesthetics, the concept of symbol involves “reflective referentiality” and transparency. In other words, the artwork, or a part thereof, is more or less transparently referring to some object or event in the world—the world external to the artwork itself. Gal prefers substituting “productive referentiality,” which produces new referents, not preexisting or preconceived referents. A productive referent is a “result of its own ‘material’ or compositional qualities” (p. 13). This is (perhaps) a cogent criticism of the linguistic aesthetics of Goodman and Danto, but it does not apply to many other theories in this tradition. Simply consider the work of Dickie, Carroll, Levinson, Kivy, and Stephen Davies from the past forty years. One detects a straw man argument. One important value of this book is Gal's demonstration of interesting and cogent comparisons between the aestheticists and the early formalists. However, many questions remain. Is there confusion about whether a theory of art should be descriptive or prescriptive or both? If prescriptive, then how can the aestheticist‐formalist insist on the freedom and autonomy that is central to these theories? It seems that the aestheticist‐formalist seeks to influence artistic practices, whereas the descriptivist approach is explanatory. To wit, given the history of artistic practices and the kinds of thing people have called art, the goal of descriptivist theories of art is to establish or acquire the essential features of art and artworks. Which is Gal pursuing? Is there an implicit acceptance of the honorific sense of “art” and a rejection of a classificatory sense? There is no outright condemnation of contemporary art, but if, for example, conceptual art cannot be subsumed under deep formalism, then one is confronted with a false dilemma. One either rejects conceptual art as art, or one is forced to pay attention to features of conceptual art that probably miss the point. The goal is to discover a way for the content to be, to a certain extent, separable from, or external to, the artwork while avoiding the substitutivity problem or dissolving it. Indeed, this is a difficult problem. Contemporary discussions of, say, which properties are part of the identity conditions of an artwork are descriptive projects. Now, there are prescriptive or normative concerns, but those have to do with what one might call meta‐ontological issues. Analytic aestheticians recognize the role that evaluation may play in developing metaphysical theories: what we value in artworks, as evidenced by critical practices, helps to determine which properties are essential to an artwork. But this valuing comes ex post facto, after the artwork has been produced; it is not meant to determine artistic practices. One learns a considerable amount of valuable information about Whistler, Pater, Wilde, Fry, and Bell. Elements of Gal's theory should be taken seriously as a bellwether. Alternative theories to the often‐unwarranted focus on reductive notions of artwork content need to be developed. And for those interested in the modern period of art and criticism, this book should be read.

title: Subversive Strategies in Chinese Avant-Garde Art
abstract: >The following review of an underground exhibition held alongside the Shanghai Biennale 2000 appeared in the July 2001 issue of Art in America. Socialist realism, which was still acknowledged in the modern portion of the Guggenheim Museum's “China, 5,000 Years” exhibition in 1998, has vanished without a trace …[China] essentially skipped the stage of modernist formalism, moving in two Great Leaps, so to speak, from traditional ink painting to Socialist Realism to postmodern eclecticism … The urge for practitioners to “catch up” with the West and to stand out from the overwhelming competition leads many to a strategy of shock. If one “Fuck Off” artist uses a dead baby (Sun Yuan in Honey, 1999, or Zhu Yu in Eating People, 2000), the next, it seems, must use two (Peng Yu [and Sun Yuan] in Link of the Body). After decades of censorship, China's young talents now seem obsessed with testing the limits of tolerance: How much provocation will the government permit? When will viewers begin to react with physical disgust or moral outrage?… These “progressives” are remarkably like avant‐garde artists everywhere … Nothing is more uniform, it seems, than art‐world nonconformity.1 It is true that nonconformity is a mark of the avant‐garde, but it can be argued, pace this review, that to read the work of Chinese nonconforming artists at the turn of the twenty‐first century as doing nothing but testing the limits of tolerance is to do the art an injustice and to deprive oneself of a lesson on the possible functions of and, hence, the nature of art. The evidence for this can be found by looking at the art of the Chinese avant‐garde as a series of subversions of the claims of certain beliefs to be true. The first subversion is of the presumption that a communist government with a capitalist economy can carve out a social space in which people can be themselves; the second, that the discourses in place in China are interpretable; and the third, that Western conceptions of art, supposing as they do a chasm between art and nature raw, can be adequate to China at the turn of the new century. This way of looking raises the question of whether there are concepts specific to a non‐Western aesthetics that have been omitted or marginalized in the West and would, were they to enter its critical discourse, enrich specific concepts in Western aesthetics and philosophies of art. More precisely, the question is whether there are traits or concepts present in the one art and absent from the other that are so deeply entrenched as not to be able to leave their context in order to enter the critical discourse of the West. An answer to this requires the separation out of the distinctly non‐Western and the transposition of what is separated out to Western criticism. In the fast‐moving history of post‐Cultural Revolution art in China there was a further forward leap from traditional ink painting to postmodern eclecticism not mentioned in the review in Art in America: from Socialist Realism to Political Pop, whose style, though not its content, was indebted to the art of the 1960s in the West. Political Pop performed the first of the three subversions through which the course of recent Chinese art can be charted. One reason to see the art as subversion is to discover what in it is global and what local. “Global” is here taken to apply to those activities or genres that can shake free of their native soil and be transported to almost anywhere, practices such as the manufacture of clothes for American companies and the analysis of radiological scans from American hospitals that have moved to China and to India, respectively, and genres such as the installations and performance art that have journeyed from New York to Beijing. A difference between the economic and aesthetic cases leads to a distinction between the global and the local: something is global when it is unmarked by its travels and local when it bears the imprint of the place to which it has traveled. For example, the “Made in China” tag is the only evidence that many articles of clothing designed and sold by American companies are not of American manufacture. The clothing could have been made anywhere, and aside from the tag there is no sign of its having come from China. The installations and performance art made by artists of the Chinese avant‐garde, however, are marked by the Chinese present and past, and their origin in the West pales in the face of their Chinese‐ness. The imported genres themselves can become so familiar as to lose their “outsider‐ness” and come to be thought of as local or homegrown. China did skip the modernist formalism that reigned in the West throughout the period bracketed by the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 and the onset of the Cultural Revolution in 1966. An art conceived as significant form, an art whose content was excoriated for distracting the viewer from the plastic values whose creation is art's purpose, is a luxury Chinese artists cannot afford. The formalist creates forms free of content, message, or meaning of any sort, forms the mere perception of which pleases. Chinese avant‐garde artists, on the other hand, perform ritualistic erasures of systems of intelligibility like language and art. In this activity lies the second subversion. It is performed for at least two different sorts of reasons. One is skepticism or cynicism or despair about, finally, the intelligibility of extant languages and arts. The other is the performance of an intellectual exercise: to find out how much content or meaning one can take away and still have anything that does more than merely please. The exercise includes an experiment in imagination: should the erasures succeed and the world be reduced to nothing but empty forms, would the artist's presence, his or her body and its gestures, be enough to remake the world? The answer from China today is yes. Part of what is distinctive about the work of the Chinese avant‐garde is its subject matter and, most important, the attitude the artist takes toward it. The subject matter of the most recent art is precisely the means through which the avant‐garde performs its third subversion. The distinctiveness, the “otherness,” led the U.K.'s International Trade Commission to find a television program to contain material that constituted an offense against good taste and decency, an offense to public feeling.2 Forty‐two viewers had objected to two pieces of performance art shown on a Channel 4 broadcast of Beijing Swings on January 2, 2003 at 11:05 p.m. One was Zhu Yu's Eating People, which contained a photograph of the artist eating the body of a dead baby, and the other was Peng Yu and Sun Yuan's Link of the Body, in which “the dead bodies of a pair of Siamese twins were smeared with the artists' blood.”3 The fact that Link of the Body was found to offend good taste and decency in Britain and yet won for its artists the 2002 young artist prize in the Contemporary Chinese Art Awards highlights one difference between the global and the local, the regional, the native, what cannot be exported or “shaken off.”4Link of the Body is weakly global in its genre because performance art originated in the West, but the attitudes, ideas, and impulses it expresses are local. Although a British commission found the broadcast of pictures of the work to offend public decency, the Chinese government apparently did not: it did not interfere with the underground exhibition alternate to the Shanghai Biennale 2000 that included Link of the Body. title: Prospects for Revisiting Film Theory From Unconscious Obscurity to Conscious Expansion
abstract: Film theory tries to examine how cinema builds up its identity since it aims at discovering the nature of the relationship between cinema and reality on one hand and between cinema and other fields on another hand. This is why, film theory is strongly interrelated with linguistics, philosophy, cultural studies and many other fields such as psychology, gender, and anthropology. Gilles Deleuze, for example, in his Cinema I, the Movement Image and Cinema II, the Time Image, revisits Heneri Bergson’s Matter and Memory by involving philosophy and semiotics to accentuate a more efficient method allowing theorists and practitioners to understand whether cinema should be analogous to reality, the stand supported by Bazin, or it should transcend this reality to reach psychological, absurd, or at least innovative modes that challenge the narrative and reinforce subjective ways of cinematic representation. This avant- gardist tendency becomes salient after the World War II, the era when philosophy of existentialism was so influential. Be that as it may, cinema in the recent era that is marked with a postmodernist trajectory assumes form of saturation since it stops providing any innovative styles. It rather repeats previous styles from classical and modernist cinema. Pastiche, Parody, and Irony are some genres used by postmodernist cinema to render these repetitions into practical modes. This marks the death of cinema, the notion that exists side by side with the death of theory, the concept that is related to academic works of Jacque Derrida, Gilles Deleuze, and Aijaz Ahmad. This dissertation aims at understanding the reason behind the mentioned cinematic saturation. It examines first the common mechanism operating within the contexts of the three main tendencies, namely classicism, modernism, and postmodernism to figure out the possibility of the saturation of this mechanism rather than the saturation of cinema per see, seeing that there are some recent film experiences that do not reflect any exhaustion. They rather suggest new promising configuration. On doing so, the researcher points out how material modes such as Marxism and existentialism have strongly been shaping the film theory throughout the three main cinematic trends though these trends apparently are described by film theorists such as Gilles Deleuze as contradicting each other. If we take into consideration the transcend mode of the newly born cinematic experience that is trying now hard to detach itself from the mentioned mechanism, the reason behind this saturation remains merely at the level of the tenacious mechanism constructing film theory. Cinema, however, can mark a fourth stage. It is in fact still in its embryonic phase if it is compared to literature for example. This dissertation works towards deconstructing the nature of this postmodernist cinematic saturation embodied in repetitions and a certain inability to create original styles. The researcher in the course of this dissertation examines the common factor of contradicted styles to find out whether this saturation is stemmed from the repetitive theory of materialism itself or is it a salient and an ultimate death to film theory and cinematic genres. Is it the end of cinema or rather a shift from agency of unconscious obscurity caught between racist ideologies and nihilist modes to a more promising formula liberating cinema from its rigid regulations and limitations? This generic amalgamation characterizing the new cinematic experience blurs the boundaries between conventional Avant-garde modes. The samples that the researcher uses to prove the birth of a newly born method construe to what extent cinema can benefit from the mixing-up of different aesthetics. This will allow cineastes to abandon the breaks and boundaries imposed by rigorous theories that continue operating within liberal theories such as feminism and post colonialism. If the reason behind this saturation is Marxism and materialism, can cinema do without them? Can it live longer? Can it construct an effective paradigm based on freedom and liberation from narrow limitations and grand narratives? Do we have the right to dream again of a multidimensional cultural construction? To conduct this dissertation, the researcher applies textual and stylistic analyses. The researcher opts for the content analysis since it is effective in dealing with the contents constructed by media, arts, communication, visual texts, and cinema. It allows the researcher to decode the coded filmic elements in the selected samples to understand and deconstruct the nature and the meaning of symbols behind the studied imagesand other suggested nuances. On understanding the specific characteristics in visual texts, the textual analysis accentuates tempo- spatial, linguistic, iconic, and thematic tools, which are all of a great importance to deconstruct meanings of these samples. Concerning the stylistic analysis, it allows the researcher to construct an idea about how these visual texts are constructed in terms of the style. The aim behind the stylistic approach is to interpret the form in relationto aesthetic filmic elements such as the camera movements, colors, costume, editing, acting methods, sound track, etc. Respecting the theoretical framework, the researcher has opted for an eclectic m ethod. Since cinema is open to so differentideas, themes, arts, methods, and aesthetics, the researcher bases his analyses to various philosophical, and aesthetic approaches such as existentialism, nihilism, Marxism, themes and principles related to film theory, cultural studies, film studies, and semiotics. All these trends help the researcher understand the nature of themes related to films under study. They also reveal various significations with reference to acting method, montage, colors, music, sound track, screenplay, etc. In regard to the findings of this dissertation, the researcher has come to the conclusion that the saturation that has recently marked film experience occurs at the level of the theory, namely Marxism and other materialist trends rather than at the level of the cinematic experience itself. On analyzing the samples, the researcher has noticed that the six films under study try to go beyond postmodernist hybridity in an attempt to consciously embrace the notion of multiplicity. This filmic tendency believes in a kind of interdisciplinary mode or rather an eclectic choice that interweaves classical principles with modernist and postmodernist characteristics. For instance, it overlaps conventional ability with avant-garde inability, objectivity with subjectivity, history with interpretation, narrative with fragmentation, material existence with energetic mode, etc. In the same vein, it turns the two contradicted trends around each other in an ascendant manner to prove that existence is neither nihilistic nor perfect.It is rather relative by nature. The researcher finds the DNA metaphor to describe this formula. The two contradictory trends are just like the DNA strands or helices that are continuously overlapped around each other. On the basis of this conclusion, the researcher coins three main expressions. The first neologism is paraoptic im ages that suggest the use of non-material existence such as energetic mode. Yimo’s Hero is a salient example that the researcher uses to show how the film director goes beyond m agical realism and Freudian psychoanalytic dreams to express the role of energy in controlling the matter. The researcher also proves this notion by referring to Einstein’s equation (E = MC2), which explains the interactivity between energy and matter. This declares the death for the pure linearity as well as for the absolute fragmentation. It rather opts for a helical vision that suggests a multiple existence with both sides: energy and matter. These multiple elements reciprocally manifest to give a kind of sparkling faces. Whenever an element gets apparent, it quickly disappears to leave the floor for the contradictory element and vise-versa. The researcher uses within this context his second neologism, that is the Fusaifisic im age. He exchange the word mosaic for fusaifisic since the first suggests the center and the margin of the image, while the second stands for interrelated and dynamic shapes that function in a reciprocal way to escape the center. The whole method is referred to as helical because it suggests this ascending overlapped movements of contradictory modes.

title: Study by Photorealism painting: Creation Studies with the analysis on the Painting Style of Chuck Close
abstract: [[abstract]]在此筆者針對查克．克羅斯的繪畫創作形式和針對亞洲照相寫實繪畫風格和技法所帶來的影響，做一仔細地探討。將查•克羅斯Chuck Close(1940-)自己的思想、喜好、及個人特質，以極具深厚的寫實技法和特殊構圖的表現手法創作出一種微觀的概念，畫面所呈現出的內容既精細又充滿了一股冷漠的氛圍，富有震撼力的作品影響了許多照相寫實藝術家。克羅斯利用噴槍達到沒有筆觸的效果，透過長時間一點點鉅細靡遺的描繪，使畫中人物的每一根髮絲、每一格毛孔、每一條細紋及臉部任何的組織紋理，表現的一覽無遺，這種需要長時間跟極大耐心的創作技法，對亞洲照相寫實藝術家的繪畫創作又帶來何種影響呢? 筆者從此論文就中尋找出一些創作元素，更進而研練、操作，藉以尋找出照相寫實主義創作元素及技法全論文共計六個章節，其要點分述如下： 一、基本論述之研究 第一章「緒論」：簡述專題之研究動機與目的，以及論文採用的研究方法、研究範圍與架構。 二、主要的研究內容 第二章介紹「照相寫實主義」(Photorealism)的起源及查克•克羅斯的創作風格與生平簡介，第三章則以亞洲照相寫實藝術家的創作風格來做分析與技法層面上的探討。 三、研究成果之論述 第四章「個人創作作品賞析」：筆者依據前面幾章的研究心得，作自我創作的實驗，並就個人的創作理念、主題、內容形式，逐一地介紹、分析。再接受了照相寫實主義與查克•克羅斯的繪畫創作之影響後，再以自我創作的系列作品，圖文並加以詮釋，表示出筆者的自我創作表現手法的運用及畫面架構。第五章「結論」：針對本次的研究心得，以及自我創作上的內省與期許，用以終結的評述。 The writer would like to examine the influences of the form of Chuck Close’s paintings on the style and technique of photorealistic painting in Asia. Chuck Close (1940- ) creates a microscopic concept with his own thinking, preferences, and personalities with profound realistic skills and special composition in his paintings, which convey detailed contents and a strong indifferent atmosphere. His powerful works exert significant influences on photo-realistic painters. Using airbrush, Close is able to achieve effects without any traces of brushstrokes. Depicting the great details over a prolonged time, he animates each hair stand, each pore, each wrinkle, and the textures of the character’s face, rendering them completely visible. It requires much patience to create with such techniques. What are the likely influences of his techniques on photorealistic paintings in Asia? The writer intends to find out certain elements in this thesis to facilitate further study, practice, and operate in order to figure out the elements and techniques of photo-realism. This thesis falls into six chapters, delineated as follow. I Literature review (The study of basic theory) Chapter 1 “Introduction” exposes the motivation and purpose of this study and the research method and research scope and framework used in this thesis. II Scope of research (Major contents of this research) Chapter 2 discusses the origins of photorealism and the life and style of Chuck Close. Chapter 3 examines the photorealistic painters in Asia and analyzes their styles and techniques. III Research findings In Chapter 4 “Personal creative idea and explication of my works” attempts to experiment with the research findings derived in the previous chapters. My own creative ideas, themes, form, and contents are discussed and analyzed in depth. Influenced by Chuck Close’s paintings, I would like to discuss a series of my works done in new techniques and new styles, with illustrations to demonstrate the writer’s expression means and composition in my new works. Chapter 5 “Conclusion” presents my introspection and expectation of my creation done with the research findings to conclude this thesis.

title: A View From the Bridge
abstract: Arthur Miller and the Alley Theatre have a long and special history. Since 1954, four Miller plays have been repeatedly staged there: Death of a Salesman in 1954, 1997, and 2012; All My Sons, 1955, 1984, 2000, and 2015; A View From the Bridge, 1957, 1989, 1999, and 2017; and The Crucible, 1959, 1994, 2005. An Enemy of the People and After the Fall were also produced in 1961 and in 2005, respectively. Miller appeared there in 1984 when he received “the first lifetime achievement Alley Award” for “enduring contributions to the theatrical arts.” Colleen Dewhurst was present for that occasion (“Arthur Miller's A View From the Bridge” 15). During the latest run of A View From the Bridge the theater website and Playbill recapped the Alley's history of Miller productions with photographs and included a five-part Miller trivia quiz. An elaborate physical display of photographs, props, and costumes was also on view on the second of three levels of foyer in this recently remodeled major regional theater. The play was presented on the Hubbard stage, off the third level of the handsome entrance where all stairs and floors were covered with bright red carpet.Upon entering Hubbard, the audience saw a bare stage with a floor of dark wood. A red telephone booth was on one side, and a small railing was close by at the front edge of the stage. The suggestion of a bridge slanted up diagonally over the set below. The foreground area was used for Alfieri's office, Eddie's interactions with other longshoremen, and the Red Hook neighborhood outside the Carbone apartment. A panel rose vertically and mechanically from the floor at the beginning of the play; an obscured view of the waterfront was projected onto it as Alfieri (Jeffrey Bean) spoke. When he finished, the panel descended into the floor, and an interior room (the ancient Greek ekkyklema device) slid forward silently and efficiently for the family apartment scenes and was retracted when the action in the community was shown.The apartment was sparsely furnished and decorated but not shabby and suited the time of the setting of the play and all the necessary action. On the back wall of the apartment a bureau stood with wall lights on both sides and a cross above it. A hanging lamp descended (and ascended as the apartment withdrew from the stage) over the dining table and chairs at stage right. An armchair stood at stage left. At front stage right a large upholstered bench appeared to be designed as a bed to be opened for visitors. The kitchen and bedrooms were accessed by one's going stage left behind the bureau wall; entrance to the apartment was located at stage right behind the dining table.What I most respect about the Alley is that it remains faithful to Miller's texts and does not attempt to update the plays or indulge in concept productions. In this production, which I saw on 13 May, we got a true representation of how life was lived in the 1950s among the working class. The characters were costumed (by Alejo Vietti) and transferred by the actors from page to stage as I had imagined them when reading the text: Marco's quiet, foreboding strength; Beatrice's helpless yet articulated concern; Catherine's sincerity and youthful exuberance; blond-haired Rodolpho's charm; Alfieri's clarity and almost painful earnestness; Eddie's otherwise solid paterfamilias lost in his unmovable resolve, headed toward tragedy. The acting remarkably related each character's personal crisis to and conflict with Eddie's obsession with Catherine: Beatrice's anguish at her diminished status as wife yet the only blood protector of her beloved niece, Catherine's thrust for independence and then a romantic future with Rodolpho, Rodolpho's striving for a life in America, Marco's rescue of his wife and children from poverty, and also the attempt of the neighbors upstairs to conceal undocumented family “submarines.”Only two minor departures from Miller's text were noted. In the text, an inebriated Eddie comes home from work, pulls three bottles of whisky from under his jacket, then discovers Catherine and Rodolpho's emerging from the bedroom, adjusting their clothes, after they hear him come home, but in this production they were fully dressed, not completing their habiliments, an act that in the text propels Eddie to attack both Catherine and Rodolpho, bringing on the crisis of the play. In the Alley production Eddie (Mark Zeisler) reacted violently, freed by his drunkenness, to the mere fact that the two young people (played by Cara Ronzetti and Jay Sullivan) were alone in the apartment. Also, in the end-of-the-play's knifing of Eddie by Marco (Frank de Julio), the otherwise strict realism of the play was slightly altered in that no blood was seen.Timely in its presentation of the current national issues of immigration; women's rights, often conflicting with the concept of the macho man; and gender or sexual orientation stereotyping; a salient and effective theme to emerge was the confluence of different types of law, connected to the lawyer Alfieri, the chorus-narrator. As a legal expert he tells the resisting Eddie that no US law will give Eddie what he wants (sole control of Catherine). The natural law of love and sexual attraction between Catherine and Rodolpho, Catherine's “daughterly” love for Eddie, and the wifely devotion of Beatrice (Josie de Guzman), despite Eddie's setting her aside, all oppose the attraction of Eddie for Catherine, itself a kind of forbidden “natural” law. The unspoken law of the community that conceals and supports undocumented immigrants, violated by Eddie when he reports Marco and Rodolpho to the authorities, is his undoing, as is the sad fate of Marco when he violates his word to Alfieri that he will not seek revenge on Eddie, thus opening himself to the serious secular and biblical law against murder. The actors smoothly played out Miller's careful intertwining of these aspects of law.When a production fulfills all audience expectations, as this one did, one is stimulated to thoughts beyond the usual concerning a play. Because the actors did not project possible individual, psychological ambiguities, noted by previous reviewers in this journal—perhaps inherent in the text of the play—and because the crisp scenic design of Hugh Landwehr and the straightforward momentum of the action were admirable, I noticed elements I had not considered before. Another set of “laws” revealed themselves to me: the genre conventions of comedy and tragedy. While Miller's intention was to write tragedy (some say revenge tragedy, but the play does not contain the characteristics of such a subgenre of tragedy) (Harmon 469), the play contains comedic lines and, more significantly, comedic plot elements as identified by Northrop Frye. Eddie's determination to control Catherine, especially in her choice of husband, resembles the irrational law of the heavy father or guardian in New Comedy, who works tirelessly but unsuccessfully against the young couple's romantic plans. Also, New Comedies end in weddings or betrothals and a final joining together and celebration of temporarily separated generations. Beatrice aids the lovers in A View From the Bridge, and their wedding will take place, now with Beatrice free to attend. However, tragedies end in estrangement of the tragic figure from family and community and finally in death, in this case Eddie's and perhaps Marco's deaths (given that Marco may receive the death penalty for his actions). Miller skillfully metamorphosed a potential New Comedy plot into layered tragedy with a double ending. In this respect the play then does, with apologies to Alfieri, “settle for half,” being half comedy and half tragedy. The entire performance was powerfully excellent and memorable, a true ensemble effort by those on the stage and those behind it.

title: The Major Female Characters in Georg Buechner's Dramas.
abstract: The treatment of the women in the plays of nine teenth-century dramatist Georg Bilchner reveals the duality inherent in his view of man and the world.On the one hand he idealizes women and presents his most positive feelings through his female characters.On the other hand, in some female characters he reveals his pessimistic view of man's determination by forces outside himself.In keeping with this duality, the women in Buchner's dramas may be divided into two distinct groups.The first group, which may be termed the idealized women, reflects tradi tional, often romantic ideals of love, purity, and faith fulness.These women--Julie and Lucile in Dantons T o d .Rosetta and Lena in Leonce and Lena--are a testimony to Biichner's satisfying relationships with the women in his own life: his mother, Caroline ReuG; and his fiancee, Wilhelmine Jaegle.While the idealized women differ greatly in characterization, all of them reflect Buchner's ideals of womanhood.V The other two female characters discussed In this study, Marion in Dantons Tod and Marie in Woyzeck.comprise the second group of women in Buchner's plays.These women are anti-idealistic both in their realistic treat ment and in the ideas implicit in their roles.In his sympathetic portrayal of these women as helpless victims of their sexuality, Btichner illustrates his deterministic view of man.The present study of the women, which includes a survey of the treatment of women and love in Buchner' s literary heritage, shows how his presentation of the female characters relates to his work in general.The
