abstract: The two books under review deal in very different ways with aspects of the production and circulation of visual imagery in mid-nineteenth century Britain. Both volumes grow out of the interest in Victorian periodicals and the art press, a field pioneered by Helene E. Roberts and the Victorian Periodicals Review (formerly Newsletter), developed by Julie F. Codell and pursued recently by Anne Helmreich and Meaghan Clarke, amongst others.1 To a significant extent this has been encouraged by the availability and searchability online of complete runs of well-known, but previously hard-to-get, titles. Just as nineteenth-century technology – and reactions to it – affected the production of journals, so too modern technology is proving highly influential in bringing a great deal of information conveniently before the researcher.2 The Art-Union was founded in 1839; in 1849 it was renamed the Art-Journal, under which title it became the single most important art publication in Britain until the advent of the Magazine of Art which ran from 1878 to1904. Its heyday, then, lay between the 1840s and about 1880, but its demise did not come until 1912. The publication was founded to pursue a number of interrelated aims: to foster knowledge of, and interest in, the history and practice of the fine and applied arts; and to promote the contemporary British school of artists, their organizations, and the market for their work. Initially it cost 8d. but this rose to 1s. in 1842 and 2s. 6d. in 1849 as the size and number of pages increased (p. 69), suggesting that its circulation, which may have reached as high as 22,000 copies per issue by 1851 (p. 51), was nevertheless socially limited. The Art-Journal and similar publications, such as the Portfolio (1870–93) and the Magazine of Art, have been studied piecemeal but Haskins's is the first sustained analysis of one publication, or rather of one aspect of its activity: the engravings that were included each month that saw it blossom and thrive. The high quality, full-page plates that appeared with most issues soon became ‘a staple of Victorian art appreciation’ (p. 11). They were commissioned from expert engravers and reproduced works by leading British artists and, to a lesser extent, their continental colleagues and the Old Masters. It is no coincidence that that, throughout its heyday, the Art-Journal was put out by Virtue and Co., one of the most prominent book and print publishers of the period, for which it would have been an important promotional tool. The theme of Haskins's book, then, is not so much a history of the Art-Journal itself as of the images that were reproduced within it. Those engravings, of which there were usually three in each issue, were printed on separate sheets of approximately A4 size; they were sometimes bound with the letterpress in annual volumes but would often have been displayed as works in their own right or perhaps gathered into portfolios, although little is known about precisely how such images were used. Nevertheless, by authorship and subject matter, the prints defined the sorts of art that should receive moral and cultural approval, and endorsed the tastes of the private collectors who frequently supplied the works that were reproduced. Many of the engravings appeared in series such as that devoted to works in the Royal Collection, and those plates were often also published in independent volumes. The engravings were hand-cut on steel plates until the 1880s when the technology of photographic reproduction began to take over. It is repeatedly pointed out that line-engraving, as it was called, was a moribund art, the life of which the Journal, preferring the artistic qualities of that technique, helped to prolong (pp. 40, 43, 45, and 110). The book sets out a readable, succinct examination of the aims of the Journal, discussing its own commentaries on the plates it reproduced and putting those plates into the wider social and artistic context. This is presented in four thematic chapters. First, it deals with the mechanics of, and the market for, ‘fine art publishing’ in a period when it was taken very seriously, for example by John Ruskin (especially pp. 52–61), both for its content and its ethical use. Second, with reference to the theory and practice of advocacy journalism, the role of the Art-Journal and its long-time editor, Samuel Carter Hall, as a promoter of Victorian art is studied. The third chapter concentrates on four series of plates, the lengthiest of which was devoted to works by J. M. W. Turner. Here, the idea of the print as a translation of a painting rather than a replication is discussed. Suffice to say that in print form many of Turner's paintings gained a degree of precision without the sacrifice of their atmospheric effects (their colour is another question entirely), making his work more readily legible (p. 134) and perhaps helping to build a popular audience for his controversial later work. The final part associates the Art-Journal with other forms of publishing for consumption in the home touching on religious imagery and the work of the highly popular animal painter, Sir Edwin Landseer. Putting to one side inevitable quibbles over details, there are some more problematic aspects to the book. We read about ‘art periodicals of the 1830s and 1840s’ (p. 67) but it is reported that in 1838 the painter Charles Landseer regretted that ‘there was no periodical publication to represent the Arts’ (p. 69). The proofreading is not of Ashgate's usual standard and even personal names are misspelt. There are confusing and even contradictory passages. For example: ‘most [of the series ‘British artists – their style and character’] were written by James Dafforne’ (p. 115), but ‘we are not certain who authored the “British Artists” series’ (p. 118). Some statements are without foundation, for example that Robert Vernon, whose collection of modern British art was presented to the nation in 1847, was an ‘arms merchant’ (p. 91). This is an exaggeration based on a myth that was debunked in 1993 in a work that is cited by Haskins.3 Many works from Vernon's collection were engraved in the Art-Journal in a series called the Vernon Gallery (1849–54), the success of which was thought by Hall to have been pivotal in securing the journal's fortunes (p. 96). The 52 illustrations are of good quality and the enlarged details showing the characteristics of the engraver's touch are especially useful. In Goldman and Cooke's collection of essays illustration means the imagery produced in relation to poetry or fiction and consumed with it. When the steel-plate engraving was in general decline around the 1860s, an alternative medium, the wood-engraving, became very popular, especially for journal illustration even though this marked the return to an old technology. The woodblock illustration had the advantage that it could be integrated with the text or used to supply a separate whole-page image; in either case it had strong graphic qualities such as clear linear features and forceful black-white contrasts. Above all, it was cheaper and faster to produce than an engraving on steel. The nine highly stimulating essays in Reading Victorian Illustration are marked by very varied interests, the topic of illustration touching on issues of industrialization and technology, styles in art, editorial practices, publication design and the mise-en-page, and the ways that textual and visual reading may be sequenced or synchronized, as well as individual artistic and literary careers. They show the methodological diversity, the editors suggest, the complex questions around illustration require (p. 11). When it comes to the interpretation of individual illustrations there are scholarly differences: some, such as Simon Cooke and Julia Thomas, produce very intense and prescriptive readings of imagery in its own right and in relation to the text, but others are much more cautious, Philip V. Allingham contending that ‘we shall probably never understand how the Victorians read the illustrations that accompanied so much of popular fiction’ (p. 159). The first essay, by Paul Goldman, is an agenda-setting piece that calls for the definition and recognition of illustration studies as a new academic discipline. Goldman, who for decades had responsibility for illustrated books in the Department of Prints and Drawings at the British Museum, is very well placed to argue such a case. Although the subject has a long history, for Goldman it comes into its own following the publication by Routledge in 1855 of William Allingham's The Music Master when, he argues, a ‘complete break was made with the style of image in illustration’ (p. 27). The contributions to that work by the Pre-Raphaelites, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, John Everett Millais, and Arthur Hughes, marked the transition from decoration to interpretation, and the addition of greater social and psychological realism (pp. 27–31). This points to a theme taken up in other essays, that in the period there was a shift from a reliance on illustrators such as Hablot K. Browne, better known as Dickens's ‘Phiz’, to the employment of artists to provide high quality illustrative material (pp. 39, 170, 180, and 189). By the advent of the twentieth century, illustrations were being exhibited and collected as works of art in their own right. This led collectors into the ‘clipping’ dilemma, having to decide whether to keep volumes intact or to remove the illustrations (pp. 197–98). Some of the 42 well-chosen illustrations are reproduced from the ‘clipped’ collection at Aberystwyth University. One common problem in producing Victorian illustration was whether they should be literal depictions of episodes described in a text, or images inspired by those texts. As Mary Elizabeth Leighton and Lisa Surridge point out, this was taken in hand by Samuel Lucas, the editor of the journal, Once a Week. He insisted that artists actually illustrated the text, making what was read and what was seen into ‘equal partners in the discourse’ (p. 138, quoting Stuart Sillars). Millais was admired by Trollope for his willingness and capacity to do just that (p. 141). Many details appear in the course of the essays, each of which it may be hoped will one day receive fuller treatment. For example, the economics of publishing is too little known, although it has to be acknowledged that, as Haskins writes in relation to Virtue & Co. and the Art-Journal, records have often been destroyed (p. 15). Many essays refer to the very important wood-engraving workshop run by the Dalziel brothers (one of whom, Margaret, was a sister). They were employed by numerous publishers including Edward Moxon for whom they engraved the well-known illustrated edition of Tennyson's Poems he published in 1857. Although an extensive archive of proofs of the Dalziels' work, ‘fundamentally the entire working record of the engraving house from 1839 to 1893’ (p. 15), is in the British Museum, written records of the company's activities are few, so its prices, profitability, and working practices remain vague. Nevertheless some intriguing glimpses emerge, for example of the relative pay rates of artists and authors. In 1862 to 1863, Once a Week paid Harriet Martineau 17s. 6d. per column of about 600 words (amounting to about £10 per installment), whereas Millais received £6 for each half-page illustration (p. 138, footnote). Haskins discusses the extent to which Victorian ‘graphic literacy’ – that is art appreciation and knowledge – was second-hand, stating that: ‘In Victorian England, one learned about art more often from reading about it and from perusing reproductions than from viewing original works directly’ (p. 3). This echoes in the present context of digitization. Online availability, whilst having obvious benefits, cannot (yet?) provide the weight, feel, and indeed smell of the original volumes. The laptop or Kindle may be a welcome facility, but an important part of the understanding of illustrated publications should surely come, whenever possible, from the physical experience of the objects themselves in their original form if they are not to be repurposed as specimens for virtual forensic examination.

title: Blumson, Ben. Resemblance and Representation: An Essay in the Philosophy of Pictures. Cambridge, UK: Open Book Publishers, 2014, 222 pp., 7 b&w illus., $52.95 cloth, $29.95 paper.
abstract: Ben Blumson's book gathers under one cover his articles on depiction published or presented over the last seven years. The result has much value. At the same time it is in certain ways frustrating. The author's aim is to provide a nuanced and technically insightful theory of depiction that in essentials runs nearly parallel to the resemblance‐based Gricean conception of depiction devised by Catharine Abell (“Canny Resemblance,” Philosophical Review 118 [2009]: 183–223). More novel are the ingenious moves Blumson makes to show an “extremely strong analogy” between depiction and description (p. 66). This takes him into regions of philosophy of language and metaphysics that most philosophical aestheticians will find forbiddingly technical. Do not expect an easy ride. Echoing a common sentiment, the book opens with the commonplace that resemblance has some role in depiction. The question is what? Theories of objective resemblance have been roundly discredited, and their more sophisticated successors, where experienced resemblance takes over from objective resemblance, have been called into serious question. Then again, some well‐developed theories avoid making resemblance fundamental. Thus Walton's theory of mimesis and Lopes's theory of aspectual recognition make it derivative or secondary. Theories aiming at pictorial semantics (Kulvicki, Greenberg) concentrate on objective resemblance of bare bones content in depiction and subject, which is certainly fundamental but far from comprehensive, since fleshing out that content is not reducible to reliance on resemblance objective or subjective. Moreover, Greenberg argues that curvilinear perspective depends on perspective transformations that systematically diverge from resemblance, an observation that challenges all resemblance‐based theories. Abell and Blumson stand athwart these currents. They attempt to show, pace Dominic Lopes (Sense and Sensibility: Evaluating Pictures, 2006, p. 26), that such criticisms and alternative developments have not rendered all such theories “historical curiosities.” (Neither mentions curvilinear depictive systems.) The range of depiction adopted by Blumson takes in figurative painting and sculpture but not abstract painting or sculpture. Virtually all photographs are in, as are program music, mime, and non‐abstract film. Allegorical presentations in prose may also be depictive. This variety enforces a higher level of abstraction in the definition of depiction than would be the case if only visual resemblance were at issue, as in the case of pictorial depiction. But the general scheme is adaptable to exclusively visual representation. According to the theory, depiction is a form of (at least partially) nonnatural representation which is never fully conventional because not arbitrary. Depictive content is conveyed by the interaction of resemblance and reference. In this respect, Blumson says, it resembles figurative rather than literal uses of language. Lewis's theory of convention does yeoman's service in guiding the development of the theory. In the standard case of depiction‐in‐use a cooperative context prevails. Makers take account of what reasonable viewers are likely to take them to mean. Experienced viewers have a large stock of relevant knowledge, from history and current context. Even neophytes have a stock sufficient for easy cases. A crowd of considerations stands ready to operate in depiction‐competent viewers by triggering their understanding of both the reference of a depiction and the properties of its subject. Thus the general picture is one of viewers being intended to recognize depictive content as what the maker intends them to recognize, and it being further intended that this recognition be mediated by the viewer noticing a resemblance. Blumson's paraphrase of his penultimate definition, in which he instantiates the abstract stipulations, conveys the general idea. “Mona Lisa depicts Lisa's smiling … because Leo[nardo] intended that the Mona Lisa's appearing a certain way … resemble Lisa's being a certain way and intended his audience to infer his communicative intentions from that resemblance” (p. 157). The “certain way” presumably refers to the appearance of the pattern of paint that depicts the smile. The larger communicative purpose may be to convey information, to express or implant an attitude, to convey a request or demand, to entertain, to induce delight or disgust—the list is as extensive as are the communicative intentions of linguistic utterances. This general idea evades the need to specify up front the sorts of resemblance, objective or subjective, that are efficacious, the extent to which the process is systematic or the sort of symbol system, if any, that underwrites it. Naturally, the full story, even at this stage of development, requires meeting many challenges. If the communicative exchange is to work, the intention cannot be secretive and the resemblance cannot be incidental; it must provide a reason for the viewer's uptake. The intention must also be (to some extent) successful. A madman's unintelligible scrawl is not a depiction even if intended and declared by the perpetrator to be one. The intended uptake often involves experienced resemblance, but Blumson expresses doubt that this is always the case. If I understand him correctly, it may consist of an idea, as when Animal Farm allegorically depicts authoritarian governments. The audience may be potential rather than extant. The effect may be the artist's and may not be envisaged in advance, as when the frustrated Apelles (actually Protogenes) angrily throws a sponge at the head of a horse he is painting and achieves the foaming effect he had been seeking. The intended communicative purpose may not aim at viewers being persuaded by the presenter's intention but only by the evidence contained in the depiction, as in photographs submitted in evidence. Depiction of something nonexistent cannot be understood via actual resemblance of surface and subject since the subject does not exist and the intuitively appealing resort to a counterfactual (would resemble if it existed) needs an explanation—in terms of what? Inexistent objects? Blumson's solution is to conceive the content of depictions in terms of states of affairs, which have the advantage of existing even if they do not obtain. Thus states of affairs of fictive subjects can resemble states of affairs of depictions of them: both are states of affairs of something being, say, red or square or whatever. A radically accidental but intelligible picture, such as a photograph unintentionally taken by an unintentionally produced device (a fine example of Blumsonian arcana) lacks intention altogether: how should it be brought into line? Easy. It is a purely natural, not a nonnatural representation and, hence, not a depiction any more than is an animal's footprint. Foregrounding depiction‐in‐use is not meant to dispense with depictive symbol systems. Acquaintance with an applicable system is a normal part of depictive competence, though the knowledge of it be partial, fallible, and largely tacit rather than explicit. But depictions that are radically novel or eccentric may not belong to any symbol system and be understandable only by knowledge of the maker's intention. That some depictions do not belong to a depictive system mirrors the situation in language where some vocalizations, such as cries of alarm, despair, or pleasure, fall outside of any linguistic system yet do not lack meaning. Blumson's pursuit of the analogy between discourse and depiction is impressive. In his view the analogy by no means cancels the obvious difference of syntactical and semantical properties separating linguistic and depictive symbol systems. Arbitrariness lies at the heart of language, whereas on the present account resemblance lies at the heart of depiction. So language is conventional in Lewis's full sense and depiction is not. The familiar Goodmanesque differentiae also apply: density (sensitivity in Kulvicki's terminology), relative repleteness, and a property Kulvicki dubs richness, which is a matter of how comprehensive the depictive system is in representing the properties of its subject in a single image. Language is famously syntactically and semantically discrete, not dense, and attenuated rather than replete; and if we match sentences of moderate length with pictures, the former are conspicuously less rich in content. For a simple object‐picture in space, though presenting its subject from a point of view, entails an infinity of other fully specific presentations from other points of view, as all good students of British empiricism know. But, granting these basic differences, Blumson argues that a deep analogy obtains. Some shared properties have already been mentioned. The most surprising connection is that both types of system are fully compositional. How so, since depictions are not composed of anything like a vocabulary of atoms comparable to words? The answer is that the parts of a picture are pictures whose content plus their arrangement determines the meaning of the whole. This means that parts come with location indices. That understood, the idea is not all that implausible. Given any depiction, if you grasp the meaning of its parts and their arrangement, then you will understand the whole and also understand the effect on the whole of rearranging its parts. It is just that few of us ever thought of picture parts that way, with some justice, since to take parts down to virtual atomicity would not produce part pictures that could be recognized. But this idea introduces the question of how to select parts that serve this purpose. They do not come preselected, as do parts of sentences. The argument concedes that some pictures are not compositional because both parts and whole are unfamiliar. Hence there is no chance of figuring out the content of the whole from the content of the parts. These cases, he avers, are like figurative uses in language, as well as nonsense phrases (Jabberwocky) and ambiguous phrases. Hence once again the analogy between depiction and language is affirmed. The formidable formal elaborations in the final definition are aimed at accommodating perspectival aspects and depiction of impossible objects in terms of possible worlds in such a way as to ensure compositionality of the standard wide‐purpose depictive systems. Assistance in grasping the drift of the perspectival issues is available in a recent article to which Blumson helpfully refers us by Gabriel Greenberg, “Beyond Resemblance” (Philosophical Review 122 [2013]: 261–263). This reader found the exposition in this article and in the same author's Ph.D. dissertation, The Semiotic Spectrum (2011, 123–131; both works available on the author's Website) more accessible than Blumson's text, partly due to the instructive diagrams Greenberg deploys. But this does not quite take us out of the woods, for additional maneuvers are needed for depictions of logical or a posteriori impossibilities in terms of possible worlds. I suspect most aestheticians will opt for the more intuitive Waltonian theory according to which fictional worlds are not in the technical sense possible worlds. The final chapter deals with the problem of grading the degree of resemblance. The context is that of depictive realism, which presumably is a matter of close resemblance, that is, resemblance in respect of many properties. The tenor of Blumson's discussion, however, is more defensive than positive. It concerns ways of removing obstacles to determining degree of resemblance (ratio of shared weighted properties to weighted properties in total). It leaves us wondering how to apply the abstract criterion. Skeptics will doubt that any demonstration can be given of a procedure that applies the abstract rule to examples of sufficient complexity and subtlety to be of much interest. As instructive and provocative as Blumson's treatment of depiction is, it leaves the reader with a number of large questions. One is this. What precisely is the relation between the various mental processes presumed by the most highly developed rival theories of depiction to operate in depiction practices? Are our notions precise enough to answer that question? For example, recognition of resemblance seems on the surface distinct from aspectual recognition of a kind or property ascribed to a subject, and that seems different from making‐believe that one's seeing the picture is seeing (in an authorized way) a given subject with this or that set of properties. But since all agree that these processes can be preconscious, how can we tell in practice which is operating or to what extent one depends upon the other? Or if the differences are in themselves valid and in principle discoverable, how closely may they be related? For instance preconscious making‐believe may be distinguishable from plain aspectual recognition yet so intimately associated with it that the two in effect occur together. Or we may move from (ostensible) recognition of content to conscious making‐believe the moment we engage more deeply with the fictional subject. Another is provoked by the continuing standoff among the rival theories, namely, whether we should expect to discover a theory that covers all actual and possible forms of depiction. Have we a theory that covers all actual and possible languages? I do not think linguistic theorists claim as much. Perhaps the best one has a right to expect is a set of theories applicable to various types of language. If so, then arguably that should be our model for further research into depiction.

title: LEVINSON, JERROLD. Aesthetic Pursuits: Essays in the Philosophy of Art. Oxford University Press, 2017, 197 pp., $55.00 cloth.
abstract: Jerrold Levinson is among the most distinguished of contemporary philosophers of art. A new book from him is a welcome event, and this collection is no exception. It is a collection of miscellanea that, as Levinson says in the Introduction, brings together essays on philosophy of art that deal with matters other than music: “literature, film, painting, humor, emotion, beauty, artistic value, and aesthetic experience” (p. 1.). (His Musical Concerns [Oxford, 2015] brings together some of his recent work on philosophy of music.) Of the thirteen essays in this volume, six were previously published and seven appear in print for the first time. Most have been written in the past decade or so, but one was published as long ago as 1993. Most of them are well worth reading. Nevertheless, there is a toss‐offedness to this volume. (The toss‐offedness even extends to the formatting: for example, without rhyme or reason, some of the essays have footnotes while others have endnotes.) Several of the essays are occasional pieces that seem a little dated. Others, while containing hints of fascinating ideas, are under‐developed. Others elaborate positions that Levinson has defended in the past without substantially breaking new ground. Many of the essays in Levinson's earlier collections, such as Music, Art, and Metaphysics (1990) and The Pleasures of Aesthetics (1996), are classics. Some of these essays: not so much. Nevertheless, given Levinson's standing in his subdiscipline and the nuggets of insight to be gleaned from the essays here collected, this is a book that should be in every library supporting research in philosophy of art. Readers find a willingness to grapple with big questions and a knack for seeing new ones. The collection begins with a short “semi‐humorous” (p. 2) piece entitled “Farewell to the Aesthetician?” In this chapter Levinson considers the possibility that aesthetic inquiry can be replaced by either the investigations of cognitive scientists, the reflections of art critics, or the ruminations of reflective artists. In the end, Levinson concludes that aestheticians do something different from what cognitive scientists, critics, and reflective artists do. In essence, aestheticians are philosophers concerned with fundamental conceptual questions that others do not really address. The second essay, “Aesthetic Contextualism,” is an essay in meta‐aesthetics. Levinson surveys aesthetics as it is pursued in contemporary analytic circles and discerns a thread that runs through the discipline. He calls it aesthetic contextualism. “Contextualism is the thesis that a work of art is an artifact of a particular sort, an object or structure that is the product of human invention at a particular time and place, by a particular individual or individuals, and that that fact has consequences for how one properly experiences, understands, and evaluates works of art” (p. 20). We find a manifestation of aesthetic contextualism in, for example, Arthur Danto's view that something can be an artwork only when the right sort of theoretical framework has been developed. (Though Levinson does not say so, any procedural definition of art, in Stephen Davies's sense of the term, is a kind of contextualism.) Kendall Walton is also a contextualist when he holds that aesthetic properties can only be attributed when one knows the category to which a work of art belongs. Next Levinson gives an account of aesthetic experience. He rejects Noël Carroll's minimalist account of aesthetic experience, according to which such experience is simply experience of certain sorts of properties. On Levinson's view, one can attend to certain aesthetic properties without the attending being aesthetic experience. He favors an account of aesthetic experience akin to that advanced by Gary Iseminger. On this account, aesthetic experience is to be analyzed in terms of the concept of appreciation or in terms of valuing some experience for its own sake. Chapter 4 turns to the question of what makes an artwork valuable. “Is an artwork valuable in virtue of the valuable experience it can afford … or is the experience that the artwork can afford us … valuable because it is an experience of a valuable artwork?” (p. 47). Levinson opts for the first of these options (aesthetic value is a response‐dependent property) and defends it against a possible objection. According to this objection, an artwork is sometimes valued qua artistic achievement rather than qua source of valuable experience. Levinson proposes that an artistic achievement of some sort (the solution of some artistic problem or the creation of a new style) is valuable if and only if the artistic achievement makes possible a new or more rewarding sort of aesthetic experience. Next Levinson goes on to consider a previously unnoticed paradox that arises from a Humean approach to aesthetic judgement. He begins by arguing that persons who are not ideal critics (in a roughly Humean sense of the term) have a rational interest in aligning their tastes with those of an ideal critic. Such critics are best able to gauge the aesthetic values of artworks and indicate which are the most aesthetically rewarding. It follows that, in an ideal world, where all persons have aligned their tastes with those of ideal critics, everyone will have the same tastes. However, this conclusion runs counter to the intuition that it is valuable for each person to have a distinctive aesthetic personality (p. 66) and, consequently, varying tastes. Hume (in “Of the Standard of Taste”), of course, had his own response to this question (actually, he stole it from Jean‐Baptiste Dubos, but that is another story): “notwithstanding all our endeavours to fix a standard of taste, and reconcile the discordant apprehensions of men, there still remain two sources of variation, which are not sufficient indeed to confound all the boundaries of beauty and deformity, but will often serve to produce a difference in the degrees of our approbation or blame. The one is the different humours of particular men; the other, the particular manners and opinions of our age and country.” On Hume's view, then, there is no danger that, even at the ideal end of aesthetic inquiry, everyone will have the same tastes. Rather than adopting this solution, Levinson opts to explore seven other solutions to the paradox in order to, if he has “made a mountain [Teneriffe, presumably] out of a molehill,” reduce it down to “manageable proportions” (p. 75). A short essay entitled “Falling in Love with a Book” ensues. We all love certain books, but, according to Levinson, the property of being lovable is not identical to the property of having a high degree of aesthetic value. Certain books (Mann's Dr. Faustus, Dostoyevsky's Crime and Punishment, and Dickens's Our Mutual Friend are among Levinson's examples) have high aesthetic value but lack the property of being lovable (possessed by, for example, David Copperfield and The Brothers Karamozov). Levinson, however, makes little progress in analyzing the concept of lovability or, indeed, convincing the reader that there is some single property of being loveable. As Wittgenstein might say, having been provided with some examples of loveable books, I cannot go on. I do not know the rule that Levinson is following. Here again, I am inclined to side with Hume: “We choose our favourite author [and the books we love] as we do our friend, from a conformity of humour and disposition.” Immoral jokes are the next item on the agenda. Levinson's concern is the tension between two apparent truths: (1) some jokes (racist, sexist, and homophobic jokes, for example) are morally objectionable; (2) some of these jokes are funny. The punch line of the joke that begins, “How many feminists does it take to change a light bulb?” is, notoriously, “That's not funny.” Levinson is interested in the question of why it is not always appropriate to respond (and respond truthfully) to a morally objectionable joke, “That's not funny.” Levinson reaches the conclusion that immoral jokes can be funny, but pronounced immorality will have an amusement‐inhibiting effect. However, there are jokes which depend on a hearer being susceptible to attitudes or beliefs that are “not entirely unthinkable” (p. 87). When this is the case, certain immoral jokes can be guilty pleasures. Chapter 8 argues that the term “beauty” does not refer to a single visible property of objects. On the contrary, Levinson identifies seven distinct sorts of visible beauty: “abstract beauty, artistic beauty, artifactual beauty, natural beauty, physical beauty, and moral beauty.” The final two sorts are “modes of human beauty” (p. 102). (Levinson entertains the possibility that this list is not exhaustive.) He is inclined to think that each of these terms refers to a different sort of property. In an exemplary display of philosophical analysis, Levinson develops a taxonomy for distinguishing between these types of beauty. Nevertheless, the topic of beauty is a vast one and this chapter reads rather like a long abstract of a book on the subject. Many important issues and questions are mentioned only in passing. I certainly hope that Levinson goes on to write a book on the subject of beauty. It would certainly be of great interest to the philosophy of art community. The next two chapters are critical notices of books: Martha Nussbaum's Upheavals of Thought (Cambridge, 2003) and Paisley Livingston's Art and Intention: A Philosophical Study (Oxford, 2005). (Strangely, full citation information for the latter volume appears nowhere in this book: another sign of toss‐offedness. For the record, it was published in Oxford by Oxford University Press.) In the first of these chapters, Levinson takes issue with Nussbaum's neo‐Stoic and cognitivist theory of emotion. Philosophy of emotion has made great strides in the past twelve to fifteen years, and it would have been nice to see an updated version of this essay that takes recent literature into account. In the chapter on Livingston, Levinson defends a doctrine with which he is closely associated (the hypothetical intentional account of interpretation) against criticisms advanced by Livingston. Chapter 11 continues the defense of hypothetical intentionalism. In particular, Levinson defends his version of this doctrine against concerns raised by Stephen Davies and Robert Stecker. The book concludes with two essays that address different aspects of film. The first of these defends the view that, in watching a film, viewers imagine that they are seeing something. For example, watching Wonder Woman (Jenkins, 2017) viewers imagine (or, in Walton's terminology, make‐believe) that they are seeing an Amazon princess. Levinson defends this view against criticisms directed against it by Gregory Currie. The final essay develops themes introduced in Levinson's earlier essay, “Film Music and Narrative Agency,” an essay included in an earlier collection of his essays, Contemplating Art (Oxford, 2002) and is designed to assist in understanding the role of sound in film. Here he introduces a distinction between “sound as design versus sound as commentary” (p. 175). The first is designed to enhance what Levinson calls experiential realism. An example of such sound is dialogue between characters in a narrative fiction film. The second sort of sound contributes to a film qua total perceptual configuration. An example is commentary in a documentary film. Sound as commentary is not common in films that are narrative fictions, but it is found in some nonstandard cinema. The second half of this essay is a study of how Levinson's distinction between sound as design and sound as commentary helps us understand a specific example of nonstandard cinema, namely, Jean‐Luc Godard's Masculin‐Feminin (1965). As the first paragraph of this review suggested, some of the essays in this collection are redolent of the back of the filing cabinet. One imagines that some of them were dusted off to bring this volume up to a suitable bulk. Nevertheless, there is much to appreciate here. Many of the hypotheses that Levinson has advanced in the course of his distinguished career have very considerable and continuing philosophical interest. Essays that elaborate these views will be important to philosophers of art who continue to test these hypotheses. Other essays broach new topics. Even when these essays cannot be considered the final word on these topics, they are often interesting and suggestive. Still, a couple of essays in this volume probably should not have seen the light of day in anything like their current form and will not enhance Levinson's well‐deserved reputation as one of the most distinguished contemporary philosophers of art.

title: The Persistence of Allegory: Drama and Neoclassicism from Shakespeare to Wagnerby brown, jane k.
abstract: Jane K. Brown's The Persistence of Allegory: Drama and Neoclassicism from Shakespeare to Wagner establishes how a consistent engagement with allegorical forms unites European drama across national and historical boundaries as well as between different arts, and how it animates neoclassicist efforts to regenerate itself in classical antiquity. With seven main chapters each focusing on a different classical revival, from the paintings of Claude Lorrain through the death of the Gesamtkunstwerk in Wagner, Brown establishes that neoclassicism encompasses comedy, clowning, the imitation of Greek tragedy, Senecanism, perspectivist and spectacular approaches to stage sets, court masque, and opera; she explains why extraordinary innovations in psychological realism—typically accorded priority in studies of neoclassicism—remain bound up with concurrent allegorical modalities. Brown makes the case that we should consider neoclassicism a flexible, synthetic form, or a “wave” of interrelated movements that by turns extend and impede each other. While the movements of the wave vary, they do so recurrently and distinctively: for in their shifting appropriation of allegory, they draw the tide of secularization and its consequences, including the composition of modern subjectivity. In her extensive coordination of works, or what she, following Goethe, calls their morphological analysis, Brown orients her study with conscientious scholarly scrutiny. Indeed, in the current context of escalating partition between and professionalization of academic disciplines, this is an almost unthinkable book; those of us who still hold the idea of a necessary connection between thorough scholarly labor and comprehensive structural interpretation must fear that it will be among the last of its kind. In order to make the rigorous argument, rather than the sweeping claim, for the subterranean unity of European drama, Brown works with texts from a remarkable number of languages; she acknowledges in the preface that she learned several of them to write this book. Before concluding that dramatic forms retain a common set of concerns, Brown investigates competing and incompatible practices within neoclassicism from the sixteenth through the nineteenth centuries, offering incisive accounts of Neoaristotelianism, Renaissance Neoplatonism, and indigenous morality plays. Thus she can make plain both how they combine and how they continue to compete, as in Shakespeare and Italian pastoral, to present an approach that comes to be integral for aesthetic and epistemological modernity. In so doing, Brown undercuts earlier explanations of domestic tragedy that rest upon the assumption of its simplistically mimetic, Aristotelian nature. Likewise, Brown's readings ultimately make clear that a more systematic grasp of the exercise of allegory and its long‐term rapport with symbol provide a fuller, more faithful understanding of Shakespeare's and Goethe's practices than scholars, including recent followers of Walter Benjamin, have been able to offer. Against Fletcher's comprehensive phenomenology of allegory as well as Shakespeare scholarship almost in toto, Brown demonstrates both that allegorical practice varies widely and historically and that allegory is a robust, enduring mode at work also in Shakespeare's plays. Brown argues that our ability to come to terms with works such as Goethe's Faust and Mozart's Die Zauberflöte depends upon our recovery of their allegorical modalities. One of this work's finest achievements is its elucidation of how the recognition of secularism emerges, confronts its historical foundations, and begins to pursue its consequences, precisely by challenging the representational forms used to signify divine Logos and its amenability to human understanding. Traditional morality plays rely upon allegorical representations to make religious ideas about an essentially fixed, divinely ordered cosmos concrete. But if the original charge of allegory is to render the supernatural visible, then the record of allegory's development is one of translations of that very religious framework into a form of representation that might still bear meaning in a world anxious about the absence or inscrutability of divinity. In the juxtaposition of morality play and Senecan formula, the admixture of mimetic and allegorical representations, and the combination of Aristotelianism and Renaissance Neoplatonism, works do not so much suppress the supernatural as labor to decode it for a world both mistrustful of religious rigidity and unnerved by its own uncertainty. Yet as Brown presents in detail, the translation of the sacrosanct is neither one‐directional nor rarefied; rather, it is as if painting and various modes of performance present the general anxiety by becoming its mode of expression. Works express the danger of secularization by recording distress, loss, and the collapse of divine order; moreover, they pursue the creative ramifications of these vacillations. By closely analyzing Shakespeare, Vondel, Racine, Jonson, Vitruvian Revival, Mozart, and Wagner, Brown establishes that the application of allegory is a decisive aspect of secularization, rather than (as the standard reading goes) a defense against it. Surveying first the pervasive historical apprehension, within allegorical forms, that an incongruity between material world and invisible spirit cannot be surmounted by aesthetic creations, Brown shows the tension cresting in the seventeenth century. Bidermann's Cenodoxus and Shakespeare's Hamlet stage the way that allegory becomes the very exemplar of theater's art of rendering visible, which thereby forces a confrontation with allegory's own theatricality or worldliness. The ensuing turn from allegory entails both recognition of its hitherto paradoxical character no less than its distillation into emblem and symbol. Yet well before critics judge allegory to be a remnant of artistic adolescence, it is already combining with mimetic forms to introduce the very possibility of modern character. Brown uncovers the emergence of character out of negotiations among allegorical and ostensibly opposing forms, ranging from the Mantegna painting of Minerva Chasing the Vices from the Garden of Virtue that graces the book's cover, to the music with which Wagner narrates the drama of interiority. Following a close study of Calderón, Brown can demonstrate how Calderón's incorporation of kingly into divine authority as well as the Counter‐Reformation's praise of the institution of the church, rather than God, produce, in effect, both secular works and works that rely on spectacle, lavish costuming, and personification allegories to bring the issue of individual character to the surface. Rendering a meticulous lineage of the notion of selfhood, Brown concludes that in mimetic drama, as in the Latinate tragedies, the self is presented first as a host of qualities, each externally extant. “They are not yet represented as a single human body. …[T]he first function of these elaborated languages of allegory is not to deny but to adapt to a more complex notion of the self” (p. 126). Complexity of character is not merely the end of a development out of allegory, for the marriage of allegory and mimesis produces the requirement of character development. In Vondel's Lucifer, a chorus represents Lucifer's divided inner life; in Racine's Iphigénie en Aulide, traditional allegorical structures are utilized to portray the pressure between self and other (p. 107). After examining a number of parallel examples, Brown is able to argue that in “a certain rough sense, all the allegorical structures of European drama have been psychological. The discussion began with … the battle of the vices and virtues for the human soul. In the course of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, under the pressure of Aristotelianism what had been vices and virtues within a widely acknowledged moral system turned into feelings, expressions of the individual” (p. 217). Yet once cosmos is sublimated irrevocably into subject, human emotions supplant the salvation still available, for example, in Calderón. Salvation, that is, becomes a matter of immanent, personal recovery or inward triumph, and as music is tied ever more to human emotion, opera emerges as a primary medium for the exploration of neoclassicism's capacity for emotive expression. By the 1770s, Brown shows, music has become the cornerstone of mimetic drama. Voltaire, too, comes to rely upon “operatic moments.” While he rejects the institution of the church, Voltaire co‐opts more traditional forms of morality and tragedy in order to attack the system that initially authorized them (p. 170). Voltaire's Olympie utilizes the opening of doors earlier associated with revelation in ancient tragedy, yet here the revelation is “not the Truth per se, but the truth about the kind of play Olympie really is” (p. 171). Just as Olympie replaces religion with love, Voltaire's Alzire replaces blatant apotheosis with human admiration, while uniting moral tradition and classical tragedy. Goethe, who writes appreciatively of tragedy's kinship with opera, likewise humanizes allegorical vision. In his Clavigo, the symmetry of natural and supernatural is balanced and terrifying—“spirits” that stare at Clavigo turn out to be living human beings, in the funeral cortege of his beloved. These ghosts represent no cosmic order; however terrible, they are undeniably “metaphors of interiority” (p. 181). The eddies of form and content associated with neoclassicism are intermixed, then, through a common concentration on the issue of truthful representation; they establish the representation of modern subjectivity in their association and create the context for the deeper dilemma whereby representation is seen to demand the exclusion of the interior subject in favor of the presentation of the natural. If this is so, then it is also true that neither the unearthing of inwardness nor the translation of fixed supernatural markers to affective if ambiguous forces is possible without their aesthetic expression. Theater, in particular, does not just record an emergent subjectivity and secularism; changing values and modes of knowledge depend on theater for their articulation. The “theater of the world” both discloses the world and helps to constitute it. Brown claims that a crisis of representation is brought on by the conflict of allegorical and mimetic styles; she treats the synthesis of allegory and mimesis in Shakespeare, Mozart, and Goethe as achievements of perfect, if momentary, balance between them, even while tracking how these achievements thematize the struggle they momentarily steady. By the time that Goethe is elaborating on Mozart to play with ever more abstract forms, his Faust no longer advances allegories of the cosmos, but of its aesthetic representation (p. 214). For Shakespeare too, the sublimation of allegory and the incorporation of the work itself into the theatrum mundi produce ostensibly superficial forms to convey fundamental truths. In The Tempest, Ariel's spirits actually tell the truth; the “insubstantial pageant” makes present the reality it would first seem to have dissolved. Likewise, Hamlet attempts to use theater, as in his staging of “The Mousetrap,” to shed light on a reality still beyond his mastery. His fraught efforts to perform an effective action of his own—to become an actor or agent in the world—are permeated with the problem of whether a play itself can be made meaningful (p. 150). Brown's book reveals the inheritance through which the theme of painting or theater in particular, and representation in general, are increasingly treated as the manifestation of a severe epistemological problem and its acknowledgment, as well as of the paradigmatically modern attempts to solve it. It is in this genealogical line that allegory is preliminary as well as persistent. Both Vondel and Racine, for example, answer a problem raised by Senecanism by enfolding allegorical content into mimetic form. They present spectators with onstage characters who find themselves seated before still another stage, whereon the allegorical representation of their own feelings take form. While we watch the mimetic representation of their response, they passionately undergo it. Mimesis envelops allegory, and literally delivers its lessons. This is how Racine, for one, unites psychology as well as ethical content with allegorical elements. With similar initiative, Jonson's masques, Calderón's autos sacramentales, and Bidermann's miracle plays use stage spectacle to make the cause of characters' affects evident. In Bidermann's Cenodoxus, people onstage honor the corpse of Cenodoxus as that of a saint, expressing confusion as the dead body cries out. The audience, however, experiences divine revelation: for via spectacular visual effects, we also see the soul of the hypocrite Cenodoxus, extended from the body onstage, crying out as it is condemned by Christ. We learn both that sin ultimately is punished in a still‐stable cosmos, and that our contemporaries may fail to see this background or grasp its deeper truth. The ability of aesthetic representation to present itself, rather than religious content, becomes central as practitioners grow increasingly critical of spectacle and increasingly curious about its source and scope of meaning. Since this is also a central concern of modern aesthetic theory and practice, and since postmodern theory has more recently arrived at the judgment of language's deep “allegorical condition,” Brown's precisely documented, astutely argued book provides not only historical grounding, but also conceptual orientation in the complex passage we seem still to be managing. Brown's book is too fastidious, too unpretentious to harp upon such a claim. Compelling connections to Shaw, Ibsen, and Strindberg are flagged toward the work's end, and attention is given early on to the preemption of allegorical forms in Cézanne and Monet, but the bulk of this book is devoted to rigorous analysis of works that appear in the sixteenth through the nineteenth centuries, ending with those of Wagner. Its fundamental case for the dynamism and depth of allegorical representation and for the profound relationship of drama to modern self‐consciousness is judiciously developed and thoroughly convincing.

title: COVER ESSAY
abstract: SEA-SEA (1970) BY GERHARD RICHTER (b. 1932) The invention of photography in 1837 changed the form and function of painting forever. No longer the optimal medium for portraiture, scientific documentation or for the production of a verisimilitude of nature and outer reality, painting was freed to become increasingly abstract, to become a medium like music or poetry, an explorer of psychological or philosophical truths and inner verities. The supposed advantages of photography, its portability, its scientific objectivity and its reproducibility, came with certain artistic losses: a physically flat surface, easily multiplied in endless copies, that cut the cord or autographic connection between the audience and the author of the work. In short, the small black and white photographs of the later nineteenth and early twentieth centuries did not seem to share “the aura” and uniqueness of a masterpiece created on canvas. To some degree, the endless multiplication and easy availability of images of Leonardo's Mona Lisa also damaged the magic of the original; one no longer needed to visit the Louvre in order to commune with La Giaconda but could easily turn to a magazine or newspaper. The power of the mass media and the world's drowning in a flood of images only became worse with the invention of moving pictures, the subject of Walter Benjamin's essential essay, “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction” (1936), the brilliant exegesis in which the concept of “aura” was first bruited and the fascistic use of mass media predicted. Benjamin also foresaw a time when everyone would become a writer rather than a reader (ie, the development of “blogs”) and all the arts would become “mass” in nature and somewhat debased.1 What he could not foresee was the invention of the hand-held video camera around 1970 and the use of computer programs to “edit” or fictionalize photography through colorization, massive enlargement and other types of manipulation. In a manner similar to the way in which painting and drawing were changed by photography, sculpture and installation have been jolted and altered by motion pictures, video and computer-generated effects. Paradoxically, the impact of these changes has been greatest on photography itself; a medium that once reveled in its differences from painting became, in the 1980s and 1990s, a substitute or “simulacrum” of painting, aping the coloristic effects and grand scale of the older medium, taking upon itself the functions of nineteenth century history painting and twentieth century surrealism and fantasy. Along the way, art photography lost its role in social documentation and much of its scientific reliability. The generation of German photographers trained in Dusseldorf by Bernd and Hilla Becher, Thomas Ruff, Candida Hofer, Thomas Struth and Andreas Gursky, as well as that American master of self-disguise Cindy Sherman, produced photographs that commented on painting by directly imitating its most classical (ie, non-tactile) effects, photographs that successfully competed for visual impact and dollars in the marketplace of ideas and artistic success. For the umpteenth time in the course of the 20th century, painting appeared to be well and truly “dead.”FIGURE: Caption not available.Into this debate on the role of photography in late Modernism and the relative importance of painting stepped Gerhard Richter (b. 1932), also once a professor in Dusseldorf, who has spent fifty years utilizing painting to comment on photography rather than the other way around. Richter has the ability to meld the technical virtuosity of a Vermeer with the conceptual brilliance of a Duchamp; in this way he has managed to recuperate all of the classical tropes of painting, its usefulness in scientific documentation, portraiture and history, its ability to fool the eye, the concept of the masterpiece and the uniqueness of the author while, at the same time, eschewing all evidence of emotion, and denying the possibility of a “signature style.” By signature style I mean all those elements of a picture like paint handling, color palette and range of subject matter, that make any authentic Monet or Rembrandt self-evidently look like a “Monet” or a “Rembrandt” whether or not the painting is signed. How and why has Richter done this? Is the chameleon-like appearance of his work simply a joke, a kind of braggadocio to prove that he can do anything he wants to do really well or a serious commentary on our largely image-mediated world? Are the cool surfaces of his paintings simply further evidence of his bloody-minded nature or are even paintings such as these susceptible to real emotions and philosophical inquiry? To begin with, Richter paints photographs, that is to say, photorealist paintings that look like photographs (he even smears his immaculate surfaces to give a hint of the optical blur produced by the lens), many of which are based on photographs he has taken or travel souvenirs and postcards or found snapshots in the meaning that Duchamp gave to his “readymade” objects. Further, Richter often paints on photographs thereby expunging the physical separation of the two media, the photographic ground contributing the representational (ie, figurative) component of the picture while his brushstrokes add the abstract portion. In Richter's hall of mirrors, it is possible to buy an original photograph he's recently made of a painting that he once painted, a painting originally based on a photograph taken or found by Richter. At times Richter has even painted wholly abstract paintings based on photographs of brushstrokes randomly made and smeared on specimen cards kept in his files and documented in his on-going project, Atlas.2 In this way and others, Richter eliminates the conceptual difference between photography and painting since all of his early work, whether wholly abstract or wholly figurative in nature is based on an image-mediated world (ie, photographs) rather than any actual experience of the real world. Richter believes in the essential equivalency of abstraction and representation; he has painted hundreds of works in each mode but rarely combines the two. His more recent abstractions have been “spontaneously” made but share the cool photographic surfaces of the earlier photo-based abstractions. His photorealist portraits and landscapes are clearly recognizable as “Richters,” so too his classic abstract paintings in acid reds, greens and blues, his color chart paintings made of random assortments of paint samples, his mirror paintings in which the viewer sees himself and his environment. In this way, Richter has put an end to the concept of the signature style and has helped inaugurate Post-Modernism, the pluralistic and self-referential artistic period in which we live. A Richter retrospective looks like a group show put on by a half-dozen emotionally cool geniuses from several different artistic schools; simply put, he is the most important painter in the contemporary world. Politics helped form him. He was fortunate to be born in Dresden, while it was still “in” East Germany; there he was forced to learn classical artistic skills in order to produce bland Soviet-style art. Like Picasso and Matisse before him, Richter draws like an angel and his color sense is acute. Eventually his repressive education would make him develop an artistic practice in which he might use his formidable talents. For a while the only work he could find was the painting of stage sets. Stultified by his environment, he escaped to the West in 1962 and, with his artistic partner Sigmar Polke (1943-2010), became greatly influenced by American Pop Art and Andy Warhol in particular. For a brief time, Richter and Polke formed one of the great artistic dyads, like Picasso and Braque, and laughingly invented a new movement called “Capitalist Realism,” a short-lived style in which paintings based on commercial products and ads were combined with a kind of “living sculpture” or performance art. As if the gallery functioned like a furniture showroom, Polke and Richter hung out on the couches all the time their pictures were shown. And Richter destroyed all of the art he had made prior to moving to the West. Almost all of his earliest surviving paintings are photorealist in nature and painted in gray tonalities, en grisaille, so as to better imitate their sources in black and white photographs. Richter invented a series of cardboard and plastic “combs” with which he could smear his perfectly made photographic copies and introduce the optical distortion of the camera lens thereby tipping off the viewer that the real subject of the painting was the physical photograph itself and not merely the object contained within it. Of course, not all photographic subjects are of equal weight; Richter is old enough to have lived through the Second World War and has close family members who belonged to the Nazi Party and served as German soldiers. One of his most famous early paintings is “Uncle Rudi” (1965), based on a family snapshot of his father's brother proudly posed and smiling in his Wehrmacht uniform. After painting a series of black and white mountains, Richter turned to the sea and produced a stunning group of canvases intended to function as seascapes (1969-1970). These are at once the most abstract and the most powerful seascapes painted since the nineteenth century, the majority of them greater than six feet on a side. They are composed of pure water and sky without evidence of ships, humans or animals. The even tonalities of white, gray and black compacted into clouds and waves above and below the horizon line increase the sense of brooding menace and produce an abstract effect like that of Rothko's exactly contemporaneous late paintings in which a single rectangle of dark color floats on either side of a horizontal line. Although all of these seascapes are beautiful and stupendous to behold, I believe that “Sea-Sea” (1970) is the most impressive of them all. The key to Richter's subterfuge is in the title, the two “seas”, and his trickery revealed in plate 194 of Atlas; the source for the painting is actually a photo-collage in which Richter has glued together the ocean from one snap to serve as the sea in his painting and the sea from another snap to serve as the sky.2 Before computer manipulated pictures became possible, Richter knew that the modern photograph could lie and so could one of his painted photographs. Of course, we want to see a stormy sky above a wave-swept sea. When visual input is inconclusive, the visual system adjusts the processing of current input on the basis of past experience; this effect can be demonstrated in both short-term and long-term situations.3 Our brains are hard-wired to make sense of the world based on incomplete information; it's a wonder that we are so often correct in our conclusions. The visual system, in particular, obeys the biological imperative to keep us safe in a world of environmental dangers and fleeing prey; its fleeting glimpses conveyed by the two optic nerves represent one third of the entire input (6 million afferent fibers) to the brain's CPU, and the brain must often complete the incomplete information it receives. Stimuli without a clear structure, like Rorschach inkblots, allow multiple interpretations, some of which depend on which visual field (ie, hemisphere) receives the information.4 Richter makes the processing of his image as difficult as possible by eliminating our expectation of a figure/ground relationship. Confronted by a visual image we seem to need a dominant shape or figure, with a definite contour, set against a background; the figure-ground relationship is one of the great discoveries of Gestalt psychology. In addition, we prefer figures that obey the gestalt law of Prägnanz, the tendency towards meaning, simplicity and completeness. In “Sea-Sea” there is uniformity above and below the horizon line with no definite figure, everything is “ground” and everything appears to be water. The hundreds of wavelets are too numerous for us to properly analyze; furthermore we expect them to move. Matisse commented that “movement thus understood corresponds to nothing in nature: when we capture it by surprise in a snapshot, the resulting image reminds us of nothing that we have seen”5; Richter has painted just such a snapshot. Spatial ambiguity in such a picture is further increased when color effects are removed and the eye must depend on the gray scale alone. In the Renaissance, wall paintings of statues situated in architectural niches were often painted in whites and grays so as to better create the illusion of shallow depth when deep shadows were not realistic or physically possible. The spatial recession in Richter's painting is similarly shallow and ambiguous; this image of “sky” and ocean hovers in its uniform treatment of “object” between the real world and the empyrean of an abstract universe, between something we know and something we're not quite sure of, like the photograph real and not-real, like the modern painting too, an object in our world and yet not completely of it. Michael Salcman, MD Baltimore, Maryland

title: Interpretation and Transformation: Explorations in Art and the Self by krausz, michael
abstract: Michael Krausz's latest book marks an important contribution to the study of interpretation as a philosophical problem that has major ramifications for fields across the arts and the humanities. The relevance of the author's concern in this volume—understanding the process of interpretation with its aims, main premises, and limitations—goes beyond the confines of the discipline of philosophy, as interpretation is part and parcel of domains such as literature, visual arts, music, and, as Krausz shows, even the conduct of our daily lives, particularly with regard to the constitution of personal identities. Krausz, then, takes on a major task, and his treatment does not disappoint the reader. He comes to this topic after several previous books dedicated to it—including Rightness and Reason: Interpretation in Cultural Practices (Cornell University Press, 1993), Limits of Rightness (Rowman and Littlefield, 2000), and Is There a Single Right Interpretation? (Penn State University Press, 2002)—as well as a detailed response to a series of studies dedicated to his work in the Festschrift Interpretation and Its Objects: Studies in the Philosophy of Michael Krausz (Rodopi, 2003). To a large extent, the discussion offered in this book emerges in response to the questions and challenges issued by the twenty‐two contributors to the Festschrift. Considering the diversity of opinions and arguments formulated in that book, a response that manages to engage them in such depth, as Krausz's does, is no small fiat. The key to the success of this ambitious project lies in the author's unique intellectual profile: A well‐known philosopher, Krausz is also an accomplished painter, an orchestra conductor with national and international experience, and a friend of the Dalai Lama. His varied interests and multidimensional identity are reflected in his ability to forge and inhabit a conceptual space that transcends the usual disciplinary and intellectual boundaries, and enables him to draw on seemingly irreconcilable approaches. The learnedness displayed in this book—not just in the domain of philosophy, but also in aesthetics, art theory and criticism, as well as Eastern thought—allows him to rely on diverse and compelling examples that confer on his arguments an increased explanatory force. In addition, Krausz's willingness to engage topics that are not commonly discussed in the Anglo‐American philosophical discourse—crucial tenets of the Buddhist and Hindu doctrines—leads to important insights into the limits of interpretation, such as the fact that the core aim of interpretation is elucidation, and that as elucidatory, interpretive activity “involves questions of admissibility and validation” (p. 121). Measuring his concepts against Eastern ideas, Krausz warns his readers that he is not endorsing those ideas per se, but rather using them as litmus tests, as in the case of his discussion of the Vedantic notion of a Supreme Self. This approach produces some very interesting results with respect to the nature of the link between interpretation and self‐identity, such as the fact that an identity project constructed in accordance with the desideratum of complete fusion with a higher entity (the Supreme Self) that deliberately resists analysis and defies options leaves no room for interpretive activity. In other words—and this is an important finding—interpretation requires conceptualization. Finally, and perhaps the most remarkable feature of this book, is the versatility of the conceptual apparatus developed by the author. Krausz is an ecumenical thinker, willing to contemplate earnestly viewpoints that come from radically different philosophical camps and to derive useful conclusions from opposing directions. His ideas can equally benefit competing philosophical outlooks because they are not the product of a rigid, preconceived schema, but rather derived from a broad overview of situations that demand interpretive activity—from practical circumstances to specialized fields in art and aesthetics. In earlier works, the author had laid the conceptual ground for the present discussion, in the form of several key notions and distinction, which I discuss below. But this latest book makes a distinct contribution insofar as it brings to resolution some questions earlier left unanswered—most notably, the connection between interpretation and ontology—while also offering a full‐fledged, and indeed compelling, discussion of the interpretive dimension of identity construction. Both are major issues in the scholarly investigation of interpretation, and the complex as well as lucid and trenchant way in which they are treated in Interpretation and Transformation: Explorations in Art and the Self makes the book all the more impressive. Over the years, Krausz has developed a conceptual framework for the study of interpretation, which relies on three constitutive elements: ideals, aims, and objects. He defines an interpretive ideal as the critical stance that allows interpreters to decide whether to accept only one (singularism) interpretation using admissibility criteria to adjudicate among competing possibilities or to show a more tolerant attitude and allow that for some objects, and under certain circumstances, multiple interpretations can be equally admissible. It is tempting to assume that multiplism obtains especially in interpretive efforts we encounter in certain domains, such as the arts, for example. Or, one might assume that singularism and multiplism are each aligned with particular metaphysical stances. Yet for Krausz, this differentiation is not field‐dependent or reducible to the more general distinction between ontological positions, such as between a realism that would insist upon developing criteria that can establish which interpretation is correct and choosing only the correct interpretation based on them, and a constructivism that would be much laxer and admit multiple possible interpretations. Indeed, one of the main contributions made by Krausz in his earlier books and reinforced in the present volume is the so‐called detachability thesis, according to which interpretative ideals are independent of a metaphysical and ontological perspective. Pressed by critics to reflect on the connection between ontology and interpretation (see Interpretation and Its Objects), Krausz offers the concept of reference frames—schemes of justification that are appropriate for particular interpretations (p. 99)—and discusses them not only as epistemic configurations based on particular criteria of validity and admissibility, but also in terms of their emotional dimension. The chief contribution of the book is the theory of identity construction and transformation advanced by the author. How does the interpretation of personal experiences, of life stories, and the events that compose them, lead to a particular understanding of one's selfhood, and to one's ability to change in a way that is both ethically responsible (that is, responsive to others’ demands and needs) and beneficial to one's own plans and aspirations? Krausz answers this important question using both reflections on his personal experience and philosophical argumentation. He recounts, for instance, a formative encounter he experienced in his youth upon paying a visit to a friend who happened to be a painter. In his friend's studio, surrounded by paintings, Krausz suddenly found himself “inhabiting the space visually depicted in them, [a space which] corresponded to and somehow forged an ‘inner space’” with which he felt somehow familiar. “I suddenly became visually much more highly sensitive,” claims the author, “and, as a consequence, needed to paint.”“Since that time,” Krausz writes further, “I have experienced the world differently” (p. 93). What the reader might find interesting in Krausz's description of this experience is his apparent lack of concern with alternative interpretations. The seeming implacability of the revelation would seem to suggest a singularist conception of the interpretation of the experience in question. Krausz's realization that he wants to become a painter is presented as an epiphany. In a “peak experience” of this kind, what is actually revealed to the person in question is an inner necessity (p. 97), defined by Krausz as a claim of this type: “I have to paint,” or “I have to make music,” or “I have to philosophize,” or “I have to write poetry,” all of these coming from painters, musicians, philosophers, and poets who define themselves in terms of their artistic vocation. In all of these cases, “the idea of self‐transformation—or, more explicitly, self‐realization—carries with it the idea of progress. But according to what measures might there be progress?” According to Krausz, “progress occurs if I come to experience more perspicuously, more expansively, more wakefully, perhaps more blissfully” (p. 98). Notice that this conception of self‐transformation is not grounded in a putative essential self. Nor should we read Krausz's revelation that he needed to paint as a discovery of an essential self. Yet the question, however, still remains: What if Krausz's interpretation of his experience in the painting studio was incorrect, and turns out to be, upon further inquiry, not the one that accurately explains the author's subsequent development as an artist and as an individual? Krausz wants us to see that this very question assumes, rather in an essentialist vein, that there is something there to be found and brought out, an “innate potentiality” more authentic than any other manifestation of the identity in question. In response to such an essentialist's position, he prefers to see potentialities in light of “pertinent narratives” (p. 104) that can be judged only in terms of their coherence, and not based on their conformity to a real state of affairs. A narrative's coherence, furthermore, can only be established within its own salient reference frame. Even when seemingly different, perhaps even competing, reference frames might be at work—such as when a person is experiencing a radical transformation in her life—there need not be one particular version of the self that is more authentic than the other. Krausz claims that “when we speak of an individual self in transition we need not assume a substantive individual self in transition exists,” but rather a self that represents a “narrative achievement” (p. 106). What is it about the narrative perspective that seems so beneficial for addressing the question of self‐identity as an interpretive project? First, the narrative perspective is neutral with respect to ontology, and thus it conforms well to the detachability thesis advanced by Krausz. Narratives do not favor either singularism or multiplism and can ultimately reckon with both. But second, and more important, the narrative framework allows a blending, and when necessary even reconciliation, of the present and the past, of the scrutinizing and the scrutinized self, thus creating a more compelling (because more comprehensive) conception of self‐identity. One can infer from Krausz's examples that such a conception of identity allows for moral responsibility while also allowing for the agency of the individuals in question, giving them the ability to be actively involved in the construction of their selfhood. Yet there are also some serious difficulties that the narrativist view of self‐identity poses. For instance, when a person posits a prior narrative self from the vantage of the present, we are dealing with a circular interpretation: The self who interprets himself in the past and the self who is interpreted are intended as one and the same entity. Since there is, as Krausz maintains, no self in the past prior to the interpretation, the interpretation institutes the past self in much the same way in which declarative utterances institute a state of affairs. To say, “I declare war on France” leads to the creation of a state of war with France. Prior to the speech act, there is no war. By this logic, however, if the interpretation creates the self, a different interpretation would also institute a different self. What is, then, the connection between the two selves—the positing and the posited ones? Krausz's answer to this query takes advantage of the detachability of a singularist or multiplist interpretation from a particular ontological position. Take, for instance, constructivism: A singularist–contructivist view of self‐identity would not entertain the notion of a preexisting self—an “essence” or a “daimon,” as other philosophers would prefer to call it—awaiting to be discovered, even though it would insist on a particular posited self as accurately represented from the perspective of the self conducting the process of inquiry. A multiplist–constructivist would be laxer in criteria of admissibility and accept instead several possible selves to be reconstructed.
